Title: How is online shopping reshaping activity patterns? Modeling activity behavior using discrete continuous models
Authors: Katherine E. Asmussen, Usman Ahmed
Abstract: This paper investigates how the rise of online shopping has reconfigured daily time–use patterns across six activity categories (online shopping, in–store shopping, at–home leisure, outside–of–home leisure, at–home maintenance, and outside–of–home maintenance) using the 2013 and 2023 waves of the American Time Use Survey. We employ a multiple discrete continuous framework to jointly estimate time–allocation parameters, decade-shift effects, and to capture complementarity and substitution effects among virtual and non–virtual, home–based and outside–of–home pursuits. Our results reveal that, while baseline shopping preferences remained stable over the decade, participation in at–home leisure and maintenance rose sharply and outside–of–home engagement declined, a likely legacy of pandemic confinement and shifting consumer expectations. Interaction effects show that online shopping complements in–store shopping and at-home leisure but substitutes for outside–of–home leisure and any type of maintenance activity. These findings highlight the need for activity-based travel demand models that more explicitly incorporate at-home and ICT-mediated behaviors, as well as for transportation and access policies that respond to the changing relationships among online shopping, in-store shopping, freight activity, and daily time use across different household and neighborhood contexts.

Title: Port environmental health Risks: Insights from the Tarragona Port-Industrial complex and planning implications
Authors: Jose L. Domingo, Joaquim Rovira, Martí Nadal
Abstract: Ports handle approximately 80% of world trade and concentrate vessels, cargo operations, and logistics that generate substantial pollution affecting nearby populations. Following a structured literature search and a narrative synthesis organized around a source-to-exposure-to-impact conceptual framework, this review evaluates the health risks associated with residential proximity to ports. Evidence consistently links port-related emissions to cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, asthma, lung cancer, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neurodevelopmental effects. The Tarragona Port is used as an illustrative example of a complex port-industrial setting in which port and co-located petrochemical emissions jointly contribute to a quantified local burden of preventable deaths and disability-adjusted life years, although the fraction attributable to port activities alone cannot be readily isolated from that of the adjacent petrochemical complex and other urban sources. These findings support targeted interventions, including mandatory Health Impact Assessments, health-based buffer zones, optimized freight routing, and real-time air quality monitoring integrated into port operations.

Title: Firm organization and worker outcomes: The role of occupational specialization
Authors: Guido Matias Cortes, Diego Dabed, Ana Oliveira, Anna Salomons
Abstract: Using matched employer-employee data from Portugal, we show that firms differ starkly in their occupational employment composition, even within detailed industries, with some firms employing workers across a broad range of occupations and others being much more specialized. These differences are robustly predictive of wages: a worker employed in an occupationally-specialized firm earns less than that same worker employed in a less specialized firm. The wage penalty for working in an occupationally-specialized firm is observed across occupations and industries of all skill levels, and is distinct from the penalty associated with working in a firm with fewer organizational layers. Specialization helps account for the role of firms in inequality, as specialization is strongly negatively related to estimated AKM firm fixed effects. Around 40%–50% of the wage penalty from specialization is explained by differences in firm productivity. Specialized firms, however, also engage in lower rates of rent-sharing conditional on productivity, accounting for up to 30% of the difference in wage premia between high- and low-specialization firms. Finally, we show that being employed in a specialized firm is also associated with worse longer-term career outcomes for workers.

Title: Reconfiguring supply chains amid geopolitical risks: a systematic review of emerging topics
Authors: Xinyue Liu, William Ho, Hugo K.S. Lam, Srinivas Talluri
Affiliations: The University of Melbourne; University of Liverpool; Michigan State University
Abstract: In recent years, geopolitical events such as Brexit and the U.S.–China trade war have become increasingly frequent and have had significant impacts on supply chains. Supply chain reconfiguration has been recognised as an effective approach to addressing geopolitical risks (GPRs). However, existing literature reviews in this field exhibit several limitations that motivate us to advance the understanding of supply chain reconfiguration amid GPRs. Accordingly, we conduct a systematic literature review of 92 high-quality journal articles published between 2015 and May 2026 to identify key emerging topics, their antecedents–decisions–outcomes (ADO) frameworks, and the associated research gaps and future research directions. Specifically, we apply a topic modelling technique combined with a semantic validation approach to classify the articles into five topics and rank their scores of emergence. This process identifies three emerging topics: supply chain reconfigurations in advanced technology sectors, adaptive risk management approaches, and diversification strategies. For each emerging topic, we develop topic-specific research frameworks using an ADO framework incorporating moderators. Based on identified gaps, we propose tailored future research directions for each emerging topic. Overall, this study advances the understanding of supply chain reconfiguration amid GPRs and provides actionable insights for future researchers and practitioners.

Title: Seeing Beauty in Ugly Produce: Do Ugly Produce Retailers Reduce Food Waste?
Authors: Zheng Han, Bin Hu, Milind Dawande
Affiliations: Driehaus College of Business DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA; Naveen Jindal School of Management University of Texas at Dallas Richardson Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Ugly produce refers to cosmetically unconventional yet taste‐ and nutrition‐wise perfectly edible produce. Advocates of ugly produce retailers claim that they help reduce food waste, but skeptics argue that ugly produce is often not wasted but meets alternative demands such as from restaurants and processed food manufacturers. Given such complications, it is necessary to model the entire produce supply chain to properly evaluate the impact of ugly produce retailers on food waste. We model an agricultural cooperative producing, pricing, and selling produce to a retailer and an alternative buyer and find that the retailer selling ugly produce indeed strictly reduces food waste. However, doing so also weakly reduces the retailer's profit, which explains traditional grocery chains' hesitancy to carry ugly produce. Fortunately, we find that a dedicated ugly produce retailer competing with a traditional retailer yields the same food waste reduction. This research reveals supply‐chain level insights into the debate about ugly produce retailers and alludes to the sustainability value of dedicated ugly produce startups.

Title: Risk-aware trading portfolio optimization
Authors: Marco Bianchetti, Gabriele D’Acunto, Gianmarco De Francisci Morales, Yuko Kuroki, Marco Scaringi, Fabio Vitale
Abstract: We investigate portfolio optimization in financial markets from a trading and risk management perspective. We term this task Risk-Aware Trading Portfolio Optimization (RATPO), formulate the corresponding optimization problem, and propose an efficient Risk-Aware Trading Swarm (RATS) algorithm to solve it. The key elements of RATPO are a generic initial portfolio $$\mathcal {P}$$ P , a specific set of Unique Eligible Instruments (UEIs), their combination into an Eligible Optimization Strategy (EOS), an objective function, and a set of constraints. RATS searches for an optimal EOS that, added to $$\mathcal {P}$$ P , improves the objective function respecting the constraints. RATS is a specialized Particle Swarm Optimization method that leverages the parameterization of $$\mathcal {P}$$ P in terms of UEIs, enables parallel computation with a large number of particles, and is fully general with respect to specific choices of the key elements, which can be customized to encode financial knowledge and needs of traders and risk managers. We showcase two RATPO applications involving a real trading portfolio made of hundreds of different financial instruments, an objective function combining both market risk (VaR) and profit&loss measures, constraints on market sensitivities and UEIs trading costs. In the case of small-sized EOS, RATS successfully identifies the optimal solution and demonstrates robustness with respect to hyper-parameters tuning. In the case of large-sized EOS, RATS markedly improves the portfolio objective value, optimizing risk and capital charge while respecting risk limits and preserving expected profits. Our work bridges the gap between the implementation of effective trading strategies and compliance with stringent regulatory and economic capital requirements, allowing a better alignment of business and risk management objectives.

Title: Diagnostic testing a time series regression with zero-one dummies
Authors: Philip Hans Franses, Mikhail Muradov
Abstract: We consider tests for normality, residual autocorrelation, and autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity for a time series regression, which includes various zero-one dummy variables for individual observations. The sizes of these tests are distorted as the residuals associated with the dummies are equal to zero. We propose a simple solution which amounts to dismissing the observations with these zero-valued residuals, that is, treat these observations as missing. With simulations we show that the resulting tests have the proper size.

Title: From scarcity to strategy: Designing hay markets to mitigate feed shortages and income shocks
Authors: Julia Kunkel, Jonathan Haag, Robert Finger, Sergei Schaub, Jürgen Groeneveld, Christian Klassert, Birgit Müller
Abstract: Grassland-based forages — such as grass, silage, and hay — are a key feed source for dairy cows. In the transition to more sustainable dairy systems, grassland-based production is increasingly valued for its contributions to biodiversity and regional resilience. However, droughts reduce grassland yields and raise feed prices, challenging farmers to secure feed and stable incomes. Existing coping strategies, such as early slaughter or livestock sales, can have long-term consequences beyond the drought event. In this study, we propose hay markets as a short-term buffer for drought-induced feed shortages and income shocks. We compare potential trading networks differing in trading radius and trading partners in terms of effectiveness, efficiency and possible side effects using a stylised network model. For farm units aggregated at the German county level, we simulate cost-minimal trading schedules and derive remaining feed shortages and income shocks. Results show that forage trading can reduce shocks by around two-third during nationwide droughts and fully mitigate localised shocks. Effective mitigation requires either a broad trading radius or sufficient trading partners. However, poorly connected nationwide networks can lead to inefficient transport, while segmentation at state level may lock in shortages and reduce both effectiveness and efficiency. We also observe unintended side effects: trading may shift income shocks to unaffected farm units and increase overall transport distances. Overall, we show that hay markets could enhance dairy farmers’ drought resistance, but must be designed carefully. Policy makers, farmer associations, and agricultural chambers can support this by providing a well-designed market infrastructure.

Title: Between resistance and readiness: Segment-specific reactions to consumption reduction
Authors: Charlotte Baar, Saskia Flachs, Petra Riefler, Oliver B. Büttner
Abstract: Limiting global warming to 1.5 °C requires not only technological innovation but also substantial reductions in individual consumption, particularly in high-income societies. Yet, sufficiency lifestyles evoke divergent expectations among individuals including gains and losses that act as enablers or barriers to adopting such lifestyles. Effective communication efforts aiming at promoting lifestyle uptake should be informed about existing consumer stances on this idea. Using a sample of Austrian consumers and latent class analysis, we identify five consumer segments that differ in their engagement with sufficiency-oriented lifestyles, from highly engaged to highly disengaged. These segments vary systematically in the benefits versus costs they anticipate from changing their lifestyles to support environmental goals. Anticipated satisfaction or frustration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs is linked to the likelihood of belonging to specific segments. The findings reveal distinct psychological profiles associated with individuals' position on sufficiency as a demand-side mitigation strategy and emphasize the importance of audience-tailored communication.

Title: Development approaches for preventing violent extremism: A systematic review of the empirical evidence
Authors: Leanne M. Kelly, Greg Barton, Anthony Ware
Abstract: This systematic review examines English-language publications documenting primary-level community programming for preventing and countering violent extremism (P/CVE) undertaken by development civil society and non-government organisations (CSO/NGOs). The objective is to identify and critically analyse the strengths, problems, gaps, and opportunities in incorporating P/CVE into international and community development work. This focus is necessary because primary-level interventions target broad community resilience, unlike secondary and tertiary interventions, which focus on at-risk or radicalised individuals. Given that development CSOs working on P/CVE programs operate independently from government-led counterterrorism efforts, this review provides insights specific to non-securitised, community-level, development-driven approaches. Source inclusion parameters were set to require empirical studies on primary-level P/CVE programs run by development CSOs. Studies of secondary and tertiary interventions, government-led programs, and initiatives by educational or religious institutions were excluded to maintain the focus on non-state, community-level, development-driven approaches. There was no restriction on location, publication date, or publication type, with both peer-reviewed and grey-literature publications included. As the P/CVE field is relatively new, it was expected that the search would mostly find publications from the 2010s and 2020s, which proved to be the case, with the earliest publication being from 2008. Records were identified using Google Scholar, Google, JSTOR Security Studies, 3ie, ALNAP, OECD iLibrary, and institutional websites, with a final search occurring on 31 January 2024. Bias was assessed by recording authors’ affiliation with the evaluand (although internal evaluations were not excluded on that basis). Extracted data was analysed using grounded theory to inductively determine themes. The systematic review incorporates 129 studies reported in 137 papers: 64% qualitative, 32% mixed-methods, and 4% quantitative. Of these, 53% were industry and evaluation reports, 31% articles, 10% books/chapters, and 6% theses. Limitations include the heterogeneity of included studies and limited evaluation rigour, which constrain reliable conclusions of program effectiveness in many papers. Grounded analysis identified three overarching thematic groupings: interconnections, power and relations, and impact. Common findings across papers highlighted the opportunities for P/CVE programming to enhance the work already being conducted by development CSOs, although papers cautioned that this needs to be carefully designed, implemented, and assessed with consideration of context, objectives, appropriate terminology, local agency, sustainability, marginalised groups, and potential for perverse outcomes. The need for consistent, long-term, untied funding of development CSOs’ P/CVE programs was frequently raised, as was the importance of prioritising local participation in all aspects of programming. Many papers noted the value of effective coordination and collaboration horizontally between communities and CSOs as well as vertically between global and local authorities and academia. Evidence of effectiveness was heterogeneous, with some studies measuring impact and others measuring satisfaction. This likely underlies a particular problem with monitoring and evaluation in this nascent field rather than necessarily representing problematic programming. Key issues with monitoring and evaluation typically include unclear and infeasible theories of change, poor monitoring practices, and limited ability to conduct rigorous evaluation due to insufficient funding and capacity. The most promising practices centred on the evaluation of changes in knowledge, attitudes, social cohesion, and wellbeing. Title: Conflict-aware seat assignment in classroom environments
Authors: Bruna Cristina Braga Charytitsch, Mariá Cristina Vasconcelos Nascimento
Abstract: Determining an effective seating plan is a key challenge in classroom management, as the spatial arrangement of students directly influences interpersonal dynamics and the overall learning environment. This paper introduces the Student Seat Allocation Problem (SSAP), which consists of strategically assigning students to seats in a traditional classroom, to minimize interpersonal conflicts while satisfying operational constraints. We propose a mathematical model and an Iterated Local Search (ILS) heuristic to address the SSAP. Computational experiments on a benchmark of 131 instances show that both methods converge to the optimal solution in 78 small- and medium-scale instances. For large-scale instances, Gurobi frequently exceeded the time limit, yet achieved very low optimality gaps, outperforming the heuristic’s average gap in 45 instances. ILS, in turn, outperformed Gurobi in 8 instances, and, when analyzing individual runs, successfully reached a gap of zero in multiple executions for several large-scale instances — within a fraction of Gurobi’s computational time. These results position ILS as an effective and accessible alternative for educational institutions where commercial solver licenses are unavailable or cost-prohibitive.

Title: Research on multi-resource flexible job shop scheduling considering flexible matching of pallets and workbenches

Title: A small volume reduction that melts down the market: Auctions with endogenous rationing
Authors: Karl-Martin Ehrhart, Ann-Katrin Fleck, Marion Ott
Abstract: Auctions with endogenous rationing have been introduced to stimulate competition. Such (procurement) auctions reduce the volume put out to tender when competition is low. This paper finds a strong negative effect of endogenous rationing on participation when bid-preparation is costly, counteracting the aim to stimulate competition. For multiple auctioneer's objectives mentioned in directives, we derive optimal mechanisms, which differ due to different evaluation of the tradeoff between participation and bid-preparation costs. Thus, the auctioneer needs to decide on an objective. However, reducing bid-preparation costs improves the optimal values of multiple objective functions.

Title: Foreign direct investment and greenhouse gas emissions: Evidence across income groups and technological contexts
Authors: Narek Mirzoyan, Jennifer Brodmann, Mahmoud Salari, Sunghoon Joo
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between foreign direct investment (FDI) and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in middle- and high-income countries. Particular attention is paid to income-group heterogeneity and the context of green technology. Using an unbalanced panel of 74 countries from 1975 to 2021, we estimate static and dynamic panel data models. The static analysis includes pooled OLS, random effects and two-way fixed effects specifications, incorporating income group and FDI-patent interactions. To address dynamic persistence and potential endogeneity, we also employ one-step and two-step system GMM estimators with lagged dependent variables and income-specific FDI effects. The results suggest a generally positive association between FDI and GHG emissions, although the magnitude and statistical significance of this relationship vary across different models. Dynamic system GMM estimations provide further evidence of a positive association between FDI and emissions. In the main interaction specifications, estimated effects are somewhat larger for middle-income economies than for high-income ones, though this difference is not consistent across all specifications and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than conclusive. Analysis of disaggregated green patent categories reveals substantial technological heterogeneity. Some patent classes are associated with a weaker FDI–emissions relationship, whereas others appear to strengthen it. In contrast, aggregate patent activity shows either positive or statistically insignificant relationships with emissions, suggesting that broad patent measures may obscure important technology-specific effects. Overall, FDI does not automatically lead to environmental improvement. Its consequences appear to vary with income-related structural conditions and the technological orientation of the host economy. These findings support broad policy caution: FDI attraction strategies should be evaluated together with environmental monitoring, and green innovation should be assessed at a more disaggregated technological level.

Title: The effect of health insurance expansion on price and demand for medications among the uninsured
Authors: Chuanzi Yue
Abstract: Social health insurance expansions can affect not only new beneficiaries but also those who remain outside the program. This paper studies these spillovers in the context of Medicare Part D. Increases in insured demand can raise or lower price depending on market conditions: they may increase price when pharmaceutical firms face less elastic demand, but reduce price when demand concentration strengthens bargaining and pass-through in competitive markets. I find that Part D lowered the out-of-pocket unit price paid by Americans under age 65 without prescription drug insurance. Price declines are larger in therapeutic classes more exposed to Part D and in classes with stronger within-class competition, consistent with a demand-concentration channel. Demand increases mainly for generic drugs and among existing users. The implied consumer-surplus gain is roughly $76 per person per year, comprising about $65 from lower price on inframarginal consumption and $11 from additional consumption. Demand responses appear strongest among lower-income, younger, and healthier uninsured individuals, consistent with greater pre-existing non-adherence. Although price fall across several drug classes, demand does not increase significantly for medications associated with greater overuse in the United States, suggesting potentially positive net health spillovers.

Title: Enhancing supply chain resilience through green investment under emerging contaminants risk: a network game theory perspective
Authors: Daipeng Ma, Jian Guan, Rui Li, Xiaohong Chen
Affiliations: Central South University; Xiangjiang Laboratory
Abstract: As emerging contaminant risks intensify, supply chains in pollution-sensitive industries have become increasingly uncertain and vulnerable. Containing pollution risk diffusion and enhancing supply chain resilience therefore constitute urgent theoretical and practical challenges. Based on inter-firm supply and demand relationships, this study constructs a network game model incorporating firm pollution sensitivity, economic exposure, and green investment. By comparing independent firm decision-making, homogeneous decision-making with network effects, and heterogeneous decision-making, this study conducts numerical simulations using data from 391 firms across six typical pollution-sensitive industries. The findings show that complementary business relationships alter the marginal returns to firms’ green investment and may induce free-riding-like strategic dependence under network externalities, thereby weakening preventive green investment incentives and increasing supply-chain network vulnerability. Firms’ green investment decisions are jointly driven by their own pollution sensitivity, potential economic losses, and partners’ risk exposure. Supply-chain topology further moderates the green investment–resilience relationship: when cooperation is limited, higher business concentration strengthens network resilience; when cooperation is intensive but structurally imbalanced, improving the green governance capacity of vulnerable firms and reducing structural asymmetry more effectively curb pollution-risk diffusion. These findings provide implications for stakeholders’ green governance and supply chain risk management decisions.

Title: Research on cascade coal procurement model based on Bi-objective and integer optimization with virtual coal blending calibration
Authors: Guangbo Wang, Jun Li, Xiaodi Huang, Yanchen Jiang, Qiansheng Li, Yongfu Wang
Affiliations: Northeastern University; HUANENG Power Intl Inc
Abstract: China’s thermal power enterprises generally rely on manual experience while lacking robust modelling and optimisation support for coal procurement, leading to non-optimal economic performance and limited feasibility of procurement schemes. To address these issues, a cascade coal procurement model with two layers is constructed. The outer loop comprehensively considers the effects of pollutant emission on coal cost, as well as seasonal-variation effect from procurement to blending on coal quality, and an improved non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (INSGA-II) is proposed for optimisation. The inner loop further considers vessel capacity and freight charges, and introduces a coal quantity adjustment and substitution mechanism to improve the original inner-loop model against the situation of “low planned coal quantity using high-capacity vessels”. Finally, a virtual coal blending model is constructed to calibrate the inner-loop scheme. Case results show that, compared with the experience-based scheme, the model-based inner-loop scheme reasonably adjusts the procurement quantity in the outer loop while ensuring supply requirements, reducing the cost by 5.75%, and the model-based virtual coal blending scheme not only optimally matches the planned load but also achieves greater economic efficiency. In addition, INSGA-II outperforms NSGA-II in cost–quality trade-off under different weights.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A neo-institutional response matrix for explaining governance dynamics influencing infrastructure project cost misperformance
Authors: Peter E. D. Love
Affiliations: School of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University
Abstract: This paper operationalizes the Fifth Hand, an emergent theory of project behavior explaining cost misperformance in infrastructure projects, through a neo-institutional response matrix that captures institutional pressure and behavioral enactment across two governance regimes: (1) the pre-contract regime, where funding commitments are established at the decision-to-build; and (2) the post-contract regime, where delivery proceeds under contractual enforcement and audit oversight. Two indices—the Mode of Action Index and the Institutional Pressure Index—classify cost-relevant decision episodes and identify patterns of dominance, transition, entrenchment, and suppression across regimes. An illustrative case, the New Perth Bunbury Highway, shows how cost trajectories emerge from governance responses to divergence between approved funding and updated cost projections. Under heightened institutional pressure, adjustments are deferred, increasing the likelihood of discrete increases in funding. Under moderated pressure, revised projections are incorporated earlier through incremental adjustment. The response matrix explains how cost misperformance develops through successive governance decisions.

Title: Blockchain technology affordances in the supply chains: a systematic literature review
Authors: Md Rokonuzzaman, Trevor Clohessy, Graham Heaslip, Sandy Schumann, George Onofrei
Affiliations: Faculty of Engineering and Computing, Atlantic Technological University Galway City; Department of Security and Crime Science, University College London; Atlantic Technological University, ATU Donegal Letterkenny

Title: Digitalisation empowering firm inventory management: a lean inventory perspective
Authors: Yang Xu, Yang Wu, Yanyan Zhang, Xu Tian
Affiliations: School of Finance, Anhui University of Finance and Economics; School of Public Policy and Administration, Nanchang University
Abstract: Drawing on a lean inventory perspective, this study examines how digitalisation empowers inventory management. Using panel data on firms listed on China’s A-share market, we find that firm digitalisation significantly increases inventory leanness, which in turn enhances firm value. Mechanism analyses show that digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency primarily through an internal optimisation channel (increasing production efficiency), and an external integration channel (enhancing supply chain efficiency). In addition, digitalisation improves inventory management efficiency by reducing sales uncertainty. This study provides empirical evidence on the mechanisms through which digitalisation empowers inventory management and enables firms to optimise inventory management and enhance firm value through digital transformation.

Title: Long short-term memory network with adapted attention mechanism for credit risk modeling
Authors: Hao Wang, Anthony Bellotti
Abstract: In recent years, survival models have received increasing attention in credit risk. Unlike classification models typically used to model defaults, survival analysis can model not only whether a borrower will default but also the time to default. Since loan transaction data are discrete time-series information, it is natural to apply a discrete-time survival model (DTSM). At the same time, there have been significant advances in deep neural networks. In this paper, we extend the DTSM using long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, incorporating an adapted LSTM-based attention mechanism to better uncover temporal features that influence the probability of default, along with a washout phase, which is used to iterate several dummy LSTM prediction steps and hence addresses the LSTM state initialization problem. Finally, instead of using a standard attention mechanism that linearly encodes the input, we adapt it with an LSTM layer that captures non-linear temporal features from the sequential data. This model shows great improvement in model fit and predictive ability, in comparison with baseline linear DTSMs and standard LSTM with attention, when evaluated on US mortgage data. Moreover, we show that our proposed model gives good forecast performance, providing practitioners with a practical and powerful early warning service to manage potential credit loss.

Title: Detecting Favoritism in Public Procurement
Authors: Joosua Virtanen, Janne Tukiainen, Susmita Baulia
Affiliations: Department of Economics Hanken School of Economics Helsinki Finland; Boulevard Tech Helsinki Finland; Department of Economics University of Turku Turku Finland; VATT Institute for Economic Research Helsinki Finland; RBB Economics Helsinki Finland
Abstract: ABSTRACT Favoritism as a mode of corruption is a major concern in public procurement (PP) in many countries. We propose a regression discontinuity design (RDD) test arguing that the winning history of marginal winners and losers can be used to detect favoritism. We apply the empirical test to PP of cleaning services in Finland and find evidence of favoritism even in this relatively low corruption environment. First, winners of close races in terms of win margin tend to have won more also in the past, which is in contrast to competitive environment. Second, to rule out an alternative explanation of collusion based on incumbency, we show that these winners also tend to submit their bids the last, indicating information sharing about rival bids from the buyer to the favored bidder.

Title: Inequality of Opportunity in Wealth: Levels, Trends and Drivers in Germany
Authors: Daniel Graeber, Johannes König, Viola Hilbert
Affiliations: DIW Berlin, IZA@LISER, CEPA Berlin Germany; BAuA/Minimum Wage Commission Information Office Berlin Germany; University of Leipzig and DIW Berlin Leipzig Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies inequality of opportunity (IOp) in individual net wealth in Germany from 2002 to 2019 using the Socio‐Economic Panel (SOEP). Applying the ex‐ante IOp framework, we quantify the share of wealth inequality attributable to immutable circumstances and benchmark it against IOp in gross labour earnings. Relative IOp in net wealth is high—slightly above one half of total wealth inequality—and stable over time, whereas relative IOp in labour earnings declines and converges towards the wealth level by the end of the study period. Decomposing net wealth into financial, real estate and business components shows similar and stable IOp levels for financial and housing wealth, but substantially higher and more variable IOp for business wealth. Across all components, childhood and parental circumstances are the dominant drivers of wealth IOp, while place effects matter most for real estate wealth and gender for business wealth. In contrast, gender and demographics are the main contributors to IOp in labour earnings.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Technology as the material ‘how’ of socio-ecological (re)production: Reflections on Wassily Leontief's ‘technological structure of the economy’
Authors: Miriam Boyer, Carlos López-Morales, Mathis Favre
Abstract: Wassily Leontief is widely known for his development of an applied approach in economics known as input-output (IO). In this paper, we turn to Leontief's analysis to reconstruct a concept of technology based on his work. The concept rests upon an analysis of Leontief's epistemological-methodological assumptions and the premises of his input-output model regarding interdependence. We argue that Leontief's concept of technology highlights the physical process of technology in two senses: As concrete flows of material stuff used in economic production in the sense of a particular ‘recipe’; but also as emergent systemic effects of that particular ‘recipe’ throughout an economy, or indeed throughout a socio-ecological system. This contrasts with other approaches in the social sciences that understand the materiality of technology largely in terms of objects, artifacts, and infrastructure. We argue that future research could benefit from incorporating Leontief's approach with work elsewhere in the social sciences. On the one hand, IO depictions of quantitative and systemic effects could be complemented by aspects that are not explicit in Leontief's framework, including specific social relations such as power, and the role of certain actors or conflicts. On the other, Leontief's emphasis on physical material aspects and their systemic effects can also link nicely with ecological research, even beyond the now common environmental extensions of the IO model. We argue that such work could yield interesting synergies in the future, not least in the field of ecological economics.

Title: When cash enters local markets: local economic spillover effects of cash transfers, remittances, and insurance
Authors: Constantin Johnen, Michael Ross Carter
Abstract: Insurance payouts, remittances, and government cash transfers all share one feature: they inject cash into local markets. While these interventions typically aim to improve the welfare of recipients, they can also affect the economic welfare of non-recipients. Yet our understanding of such economic spillover effects remains limited. Empirical studies report mixed findings, ranging from welfare-increasing to welfare-decreasing spillover effects, while the theoretical literature discussing potential mechanisms remains fragmented and lacks an integrated framework. This study develops a structured conceptual synthesis that integrates dispersed theoretical and empirical insights on the spillover effects of cash injections. We first develop a unified theoretical framework identifying the key mechanisms and moderating factors shaping spillovers, and then review the empirical literature through its lens. The framework highlights that spillover effects emerge through changes in local prices, wages, and resource sharing within social networks. We further show that the magnitude and direction of these effects depend on the interaction between cash-injection-specific parameters and the local environment, including its local economic structure and the constraints that recipient and non-recipient households face. By integrating insights across studies on cash transfers, remittances, and insurance programs, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for understanding spillover patterns of cash injections more broadly. Our analysis generates policy-relevant insights and highlights several important gaps in the current literature.

Title: Editorial Board
Capital reallocation under climate policy uncertainty
Authors: Makram Khalil, Felix Strobel
Abstract: In a structural dynamic model that incorporates two broad production sectors with different carbon emissions, we find that climate policy uncertainty (CPU) shocks (i) lower the market value of the highly carbon-emitting sector relative to the low carbon-emitting sector, and (ii) reduce real investment and the capital stock in the highly carbon-emitting sector, while real investment in the sector with low carbon emissions tends to fare better. To apply the theoretical predictions to the data, we employ a news article-based measure of climate policy uncertainty to identify CPU shocks as well as quarterly balance sheet data of listed firms in the United States. In line with the predictions from the theoretical model, we find that in response to CPU shocks (i) financial markets markedly revalue strongly carbon-emitting firms relative to firms with low carbon emissions, and (ii) substantial investment reallocation takes place, in particular from the manufacturing sector towards services.

Title: Process operating performance evaluation for IC packaging in smart manufacturing
Authors: Kuen-Suan Chen, Chun-Min Yu
Abstract: Improving the quality and yield of integrated circuit packaging processes is crucial for reducing scrap rates and component failures. Among all stages of the packaging chain, gold wire bonding is widely considered a critical process with a clearly defined role. According to the Taguchi loss function, insufficient gold wire bonding capability significantly degrades the performance of integrated circuit components, leading to premature failure. Due to the indispensable role of integrated circuit components in applications such as network communications, consumer electronics, and the automotive, industrial, aerospace, and defense sectors, any failure could disrupt operations, cause economic losses, and increase carbon emissions. This makes rapid decision-making essential and has led to a growing trend towards decision-making based on small sample sizes. Furthermore, the increasingly mature smart manufacturing environment and the continuous advancements in the Internet of Things as well as production data collection and analysis technologies have facilitated the accumulation of past professional data experience within the industry. This study thus proposes a confidence interval-based fuzzy evaluation method to establish a fuzzy evaluation model for the operational performance of integrated circuit components based on gold wire bonding process capability. Given that this method integrates previously accumulated professional data and experience and is based on confidence intervals, not only can the accuracy of decision-making be maintained, but the risk of misjudgment due to sampling errors even with a small sample size can also be reduced.

Title: Regulating investments when both costs and need are private
Authors: Daniel F. Garrett, Elena Panova
Abstract: Large-scale infrastructure investments are often carried out in settings where their eventual usefulness or importance is difficult to predict. This paper studies optimal incentives for investment when the agent undertaking the investment has superior information on two dimensions: the cost of investment and the likelihood it is useful or beneficial to the principal. Usefulness eventually becomes public, but punishments are limited as the regulator aims at ensuring the agent earns non-negative profits in each period. We characterize the optimal incentive scheme and show it involves either: (i) investments by the agent even though he knows they are useless and rents to only cost-efficient types, or (ii) rents to all types. The possibility that rent is left to all types contrasts with the usual prediction in static (and also dynamic) mechanism design and arises even though the agent’s preferences are stable over time.

Title: Asymmetric Pass‐Through and Competition
Authors: Christos Genakos, Yuan Lyu, Mario Pagliero
Affiliations: Cambridge Judge Business School, CEP and CEPR University of Cambridge Cambridge UK; School of Applied Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; Center for Research on Global Energy Strategy (CROGES) Renmin University of China Beijing China; Collegio Carlo Alberto, and CEPR University of Turin Turin Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the retail price pass‐through of four major tax changes in petroleum products using daily pricing data from gas stations on small Greek islands. We find that (i) the pass‐through of the tax hikes is five times higher than for the tax decrease, (ii) the pass‐through of the tax hikes increases with competition, while that of the tax decrease does not, (iii) there is significant asymmetry in the speed of price adjustments, and (iv) the asymmetric price adjustment can be rationalized by either tacit collusion or consumer search behavior, as the most plausible explanations.

Title: Economic Growth Vulnerability Across Euro Area Countries
Authors: Claudio Lissona, Esther Ruiz
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Bologna Bologna Italy; Department of Statistics Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Madrid Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT We analyse growth vulnerability in the four largest Euro Area (EA) economies, measured as a lower quantile of the growth distribution conditional on EA‐wide and country‐specific macroeconomic/financial factors. Growth densities are obtained under a normal activity scenario and under stressed conditions. We find that vulnerability is higher in Germany, more exposed to EA‐wide conditions, and in Spain, with large country‐specific dynamics. Under stress, financial factors amplify adverse macroeconomic conditions, and even severe individual shocks fail to fully explain the vulnerability observed under systemic stress. Our results underscore the importance of monitoring local and EA‐wide macro‐financial conditions to mitigate vulnerability.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Building resilient product portfolios in B2B manufacturing: A multi-criteria decision-making framework for managing disruptive factors
Authors: Till Gramberg, Aron Burgel, Andreas Eggert, Thomas Bauernhansl
Abstract: This study develops a methodologically grounded decision-support framework for product portfolio management (PPM) in manufacturing business-to-business (B2B) firms, aimed at systematically addressing the growing challenges posed by disruptive change, particularly those arising from digital and sustainable transformations. A preliminary study and systematic literature review reveal that current evaluation approaches fall short in addressing these emerging challenges. To address this gap, the proposed PPM-specific framework integrates established multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: the analytic hierarchy process (AHP), the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL), and the weighted sum model (WSM). In addition to the three established PPM target dimensions – value maximization, strategic fit, and balance – the proposed methodology introduces a fourth dimension: resilience to disruptive factors. This expanded framework enables a structured derivation and weighting of evaluation criteria, identification of interdependencies within the product portfolio, and a systematic assessment of the strategic value contribution of individual portfolio elements. A case study with a global automation technology provider and evaluation workshops with three additional globally operating B2B industrial firms demonstrate the framework's practical relevance. The results indicate enhanced transparency, more objective decision-making, and systematic portfolio governance. This research contributes a formal and transparent decision support tool that facilitates strategically robust portfolio design in times of disruptive transformation, thereby addressing critical gaps in existing literature.

Title: The effect of network degree on bargaining: Experimental evidence from the field
Authors: Ben D’Exelle, Christine Gutekunst, Arno Riedl
Abstract: We conduct an artefactual field experiment in real-existing trade networks to analyze how individual network degree affects bargaining demands and outcomes. We combine data from a bilateral bargaining experiment with data of trade networks in 24 villages in Uganda. To identify the effect of individual degree in the village trade network we experimentally vary the disclosure of participants’ identities in a bargaining pair. We derive hypotheses on how degree should affect behavior and find partial support for them. Specifically, we observe that individual degree affects bargaining demands in the predicted direction when one of the bargainers is informed about the network positions but not when both sides are informed. Moreover, network degree affects the likelihood of agreements and earnings, irrespective of the knowledge of the network positions of bargaining partners.

Title: Can policy design build trust in local taxation? Experimental evidence of property taxation in Mexican municipalities
Authors: Aurora Echavarria
Abstract: Property taxes, the primary source of local revenue for municipal governments, are essential for improving urban service provision and resident welfare. Yet this tax is widely unpopular and often politically contentiuous. This study's descriptive findings reveal that property owners are not currently motivated to pay their property taxes by the promise of collective benefits, but rather by the desire to secure their property rights. Thus, this study asks: What dimensions of property tax design do property owners prioritize? How do they negotiate trade-offs? And can policy design establish credible commitment? I address these questions using an experimental conjoint survey with over 2,000 property owners in 34 urban municipalities in Mexico. I find that property owners are largely indifferent to the progressivity of property tax increases yet strongly prioritize policies that enhance accountability in how government administers, spends, and enforces taxes. Specifically, the presence of active oversight strategies in the use of funds increases the support for a policy by 11 percentage points, an effect greater than that of policies that offer more direct benefits. Individuals with high perceptions of government corruption disproportionately favor tax policies that incorporate active transparency strategies even if this implies a higher fiscal burden. Overall, this study demonstrates that public support for property taxation is not entirely inelastic and that adopting accountability measures that signal how funds are spent can make property owners more accepting of tax increases. This study contributes to literature on the fiscal contract by demonstrating how policy designs that enhance accountability can help establish credible commitment.

Title: Partisan politics and sectoral policy in Africa’s agro-export commodity chains
Authors: Catherine Boone, Michael Mugisha

Title: Migration opportunities and human capital investments
Authors: Esther Gehrke
Abstract: We examine how shocks to migration opportunities affect schooling outcomes in origin communities. We focus on the migration between Mexico and the United States, and exploit the expansion of the Secure Communities program in the US—a federal data-sharing program that substantially increased the risk of deportation for illegal migrants—as an exogenous shock to the attractiveness of illegal migration. Our results suggest that the Secure Communities program increased attendance, enrollment, and educational attainment in municipalities that had stronger migration-network links with counties in the US that adopted the program early-on relative to municipalities that had ties with US counties that introduced the policy somewhat later. These results are consistent with the interpretation that the Secure Communities program raised the returns to education for prospective migrants by making low-skill migration to the US less attractive.

Title: Energy prices, inflation, and the ECB’s monetary policy during the 2021–22 energy crisis
Authors: Stefano Neri

Title: Policy pathways for low-carbon transport in Ireland: Carbon taxes and ICE bans
Authors: Daniel Cassidy, Kelly de Bruin
Abstract: This paper develops I3E-Transport, a new Irish passenger transport model that integrates behavioural, technological, and macroeconomic drivers to assess the effectiveness of carbon taxation and internal combustion engine (ICE) phase-out policies on emissions from private cars and public transport. The model is soft linked to the Ireland Environment-Energy-Economy (I3E) CGE framework, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of how these policy measures influence transport demand, vehicle stock composition, energy consumption and emissions within the passenger transport sector. Simulations for 2024–2050 indicate that, under a business-as-usual scenario, emissions rise by 2050 despite modest gains in energy efficiency and alternative vehicle uptake. A carbon tax yields only limited abatement, whereas a comprehensive ICE ban from 2035—banning hybrids—reduces CO 2 emissions by over five million tonnes relative to the baseline by 2050. However, the results show that the sector remains off track relative to implied carbon budget ceilings under a 2035 implementation, with only an earlier and comprehensive ban delivering substantial progress towards compliance, pointing to the need for timely and coordinated policy action to align Ireland’s transport sector with its long-term climate commitments.

Title: Drivers of Digital Traceability System Adoption for Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Complex Supply Chains
Authors: Sukrit Vinayavekhin, Aneesh Banerjee, Feng Li, Davide Luzzini
Affiliations: Thammasat Business School Thammasat University Bangkok Thailand; Bayes Business School (formerly Cass) City St George's University of London London UK; EADA Business School Barcelona Spain; Business School LUT University Lappeenranta Finland
Abstract: ABSTRACT The global climate crisis is pushing firms toward sustainable supply chain practices, with digital technology offering a vital pathway to track greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This research investigates the factors influencing the adoption of digital traceability systems for managing these emissions, focusing on implementation scope and supply chain complexity (SCC). Drawing on Institutional Theory and Transaction Cost Economics, we conducted a choice‐based conjoint experiment with managers in manufacturing sectors to capture the trade‐offs in their decision‐making process. Our results show that firms are more likely to consider technology solutions when (a) those solutions cover Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions, and (b) there is greater SCC due to ‘detail‐numerousness’ (number of elements in a system) and ‘detail‐variety’ (heterogeneity of these elements). However, dynamic complexity (changing nature of elements) has an ambiguous impact on technology adoption. “Detail‐numerousness” (e.g., number of products produced) is the most critical attribute for internal operations, while “detail‐variety” (e.g., geographical dispersion and supplier heterogeneity) has the greatest impact on upstream supply chains. This research extends the supply chain technology adoption literature by providing a nuanced empirical understanding of how distinct dimensions of SCC at both internal and upstream levels shape the adoption of digital traceability.

Title: “Girls with girls”: gender composition and team performance in survey data collection
Authors: Qing Huang, Yingyue Quan

Title: Why are the youngest in class more often prescribed pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
Authors: Catia Nicodemo, Cheti Nicoletti, Joaquim Vidiella-Martin
Abstract: Abstract Children who start school at a younger age are more likely to receive pharmacological treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This pattern is widely attributed to peer-comparison biases, but the relative importance of different underlying mechanisms remains debated. We use administrative data from England to study how school starting age affects ADHD prescription rates from ages 5 to 15. Exploiting a sharp school-entry cutoff and comparing children born just before and after September 1, we estimate both age- and grade-specific effects of early school entry. We find that early starters are 40–50% more likely to be treated for ADHD by age 15. This long-term gap is entirely driven by first-time prescriptions among children aged 5 to 8. Using a novel decomposition strategy, we isolate the roles of relative age, absolute age, the length of school exposure, and age at school entry. We find that relative age is the primary long-term driver, aligning with previous evidence on peer-comparison bias, while absolute age and the length of school exposure have only short-lived effects. Our findings suggest that early starters are more likely to receive marginal diagnoses due to their relative immaturity, and we recommend refining diagnostic guidelines and classroom grouping practices to reduce diagnostic gaps.

Title: Puzzles and dynamics in resource allocation: An introduction
Authors: Changxia Ke, Lucas Rentschler, Shane D. Sanders

Title: Integrated large language models and digital twin-based decision support in closed-loop supply chain operations: green steel transition case study
Authors: Chi An Le, Devika Kannan, Kannan Govindan, Truong Thinh Nguyen
Affiliations: Adelaide University
Abstract: The green steel transition requires corporates to operate closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs) that involve operational decisions under heterogeneous data. Although decision models have shifted CLSC operations towards advanced analytics and optimisation, challenges remain in automatically interpreting natural-language requests, enabling data-driven reasoning, and communicating outcomes for actionable decision-making. Motivated by recent progress in large language models (LLMs), we propose an intelligent digital twin-based decision-support method (LMiDTSC) to automatically interpret, reason, and address CLSC operational tasks, and synchronise physical and digital CLSC resources. We develop a knowledge graph, a benchmark, and an accurate query-explanation consistency (AQEC) metric to operate the method and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting decisions on steel distribution and scrap collection. Across focal operational tasks, LMiDTSC outperforms baselines (e.g. GPT-5.2) by 82.73% in AQEC, while its fine-tune outperforms backbones using proprietary models by 93.17% in AQEC. This study advances decision support systems and AI-enabled operations research by integrating LLMs and digital twins for computerised decisions in CLSC operations. This study suggests supply chain practitioners should consider high-performing LLMs for complex operational tasks and exercise caution in scaling in-context learning prompts. Finally, policymakers can accelerate the implementation of such integrated decision support systems by promoting industrial symbiosis and workforce training.

Title: Supply-demand uncertainty in bone China supply chains: distributionally robust optimization with voluntary and recycled resources
Authors: Hadi Hassanzadeh, Hossein Neghabi
Affiliations: Ferdowsi University of Mashhad
Abstract: This paper dvelops a mathematical model for designing a multi-echelon Bone China Supply Chain (BCSC), aiming to minimise total costs minus revenues through decisions related to facility location, supplier selection, and material flow quantities across the network. The model explicitly incorporates simultaneous uncertainty in both raw material supply and product demand, which is addressed using a Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) approach. Additionally, part of the required raw material is obtained through voluntarily contributed recycled sources. To solve the proposed model, we employ the L-shaped Benders decomposition algorithm and an enhanced version that incorporates a warm-up strategy to improve computational efficiency. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves higher profitability and better demand fulfillment rates under various uncertainty scenarios compared to traditional stochastic optimisation methods. Moreover, the inclusion of voluntary recycled inputs significantly reduces operational costs and enhances the overall economic performance of the BCSC. The results also confirm the effectiveness of the warm-up strategy in accelerating convergence and improving solution quality, particularly in large-scale instances.

Title: A review of process planning from an operations research perspective: models, algorithms, and benchmarks
Authors: Yiming Ma, Kaiping Luo, Qiuhong Zhao, Lianyu Zheng
Affiliations: Beihang University; Management and Decision (Beihang University), Ministry of Education
Abstract: Process planning bridges product design and manufacturing and increasingly involves multiple types of flexibility. As an NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problem, it poses substantial methodological challenges, yet effective optimisation is critical for improving production performance. This paper presents a review of process planning from an operations research perspective, covering models, algorithms, and benchmarks. We systematically classify mathematical programming models according to key characteristics, including model class, flexibility types, and objective settings, and highlight recent advances in linearisation techniques and compact formulations. From an algorithmic standpoint, we review and categorise solution paradigms, encompassing metaheuristics, multi-objective optimisation, deterministic methods, heuristics, and reinforcement learning, and analyse their respective strengths and limitations. In addition, we compile benchmark test cases together with technical specifications and best-known solutions to support systematic performance comparison. Finally, we identify research gaps and outline promising future directions, with particular emphasis on advanced optimisation methods and practically relevant modelling.

Title: Hierarchical collaborative scheduling in cloud manufacturing based on dynamic contract net protocol and deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Xi Wang, Yongkui Liu, Chunfu Zhong, Lihui Wang, Bin Zi, Yueqin Huo, Wenxue Wang
Affiliations: Xidian University; KTH Royal Institute of Technology; China National Heavy Machinery Research Institute Co., Ltd.; Chongqing University
Abstract: Cloud manufacturing facilitates collaborative production by integrating distributed manufacturing resources via service-oriented platforms. However, its scheduling process is constrained by resource heterogeneity, complex task dependencies, and inefficient platform-enterprise coordination. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach for multi-task scheduling that integrates a contract net protocol (CNP) with graph neural networks (GNNs). First, a platform-enterprise collaborative scheduling framework is proposed. Then, two CNP-based schemes are designed and extended into a Dynamic CNP (DCNP) which updates evaluation weights to improved service selection. Moreover, an RGCN-LDDQN algorithm is proposed, which integrates relational graph convolutional networks (RGCN), long short-term memory (LSTM), and double deep Q-network (DDQN) to model inter-task dependencies and support global scheduling decisions. A bi-level priority constraint is integrated to mitigate conflicts, and a priority-aware P-RGCN-LDDQN is obtained, which enhances feasibility and stability. Subtasks are autonomously scheduled using a genetic algorithm at the enterprise layer based on platform-issued objectives and constraints. Simulations with respect to automotive parts assembly tasks are conducted. Results indicate that, under DCNP, RGCN-LDDQN reduces makespan by 21.88% and comprehensive cost by 15.64% compared to conventional DDQN, while maintaining service quality. Additionally, P-RGCN-LDDQN achieves further reductions of 9.15% and 6.69% over RGCN-LDDQN.

Title: From reference class forecasting to decomposed contingency in infrastructure projects
Authors: Peter E. D. Love
Affiliations: School of Civil & Mechanical Engineering, Curtin University
Abstract: Reference class forecasting (RCF) has become a central tool in infrastructure investment governance, primarily supporting funding approval by comparing outcomes with those of completed projects. Cost overruns that arise between funding commitment and contract award, and subsequently during construction, are often tied to how risk and uncertainty are managed after project approval, particularly when RCF is used to set or control contingency allowances. These patterns point to a problem in post-approval uncertainty management rather than a limitation of cost-estimation methods alone. While RCF provides a useful assurance mechanism for testing the plausibility of proposed cost estimates, it is not designed to manage uncertainty during the pre-contract phase, when project-specific information remains incomplete and subject to revision. A decomposed contingency approach (DCA) is proposed as a conceptual and methodological framework for managing uncertainty during this period. The DCA distinguishes among risk and aleatory uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty arising from incomplete or provisional information, and residual uncertainty associated with system-level effects that cannot be fully anticipated. It links different forms of uncertainty to decision approaches suited to their informational characteristics and provides a structured basis for adjusting contingency as information becomes more complete. Within this framework, contingency is determined through a decomposed treatment of uncertainty, while RCF is retained solely as an independent assurance mechanism.

Title: Group buying strategy in dual-channel with consideration of two selling formats: reselling and agency
Authors: Mengyao Zhang, Zenghui Su, Ke Han
Abstract: Group buying platforms have emerged as well-structured marketplaces, attracting a significant number of consumers with attractive prices. While these platforms boost sellers’ sales through the group buying channel, they also create channel conflict by competing with the seller’s original channel. Consequently, sellers and group buying platforms must carefully deliberate on their cooperation modes: reselling or agency contract. Previous research has insufficiently explored how sellers and platforms select cooperation contracts in dual-channel settings. To address this gap, we construct a game-theoretical model to analyze the strategic interactions between sellers and platforms in a dual-channel structure under two different contracts. Our findings reveal several notable insights. First, under both contracts, prices in both channels decrease as peer influence efficiency increases. However, the impact of group buying effort costs on prices is nonuniform, diverging from prior findings. Second, both sellers and platforms benefit from peer influence, shedding light on the emphasis stakeholders place on leveraging peer influence in group buying strategies. Most importantly, we find that both parties are more inclined to adopt the agency contract only when the fixed commission rate is moderate. Finally, while competition between the group buying and direct channels intensifies under the agency contract, the overall performance of the supply chain improves.

Title: Mergers when price and quality are set by bargaining
Authors: David J. Balan, Jeremy A. Sandford
Affiliations: Econ One Research Washington DC USA; Econic Partners Washington DC USA
Abstract: Abstract We study the effects of horizontal mergers on product quality in a bilateral bargaining environment. In our model, a competition‐reducing merger reduces equilibrium quality as long as the buyer's marginal rate of substitution of quality for price declines with price, holding quality constant. This condition is closely related to quality being a normal good. This result holds when price and quality are jointly negotiated, and it extends to a sequential setting in which sellers first choose quality and then bargain with buyers over price. We discuss applications to procurement and healthcare markets, as well as several extensions.

Title: Financial suicide: Debt and death across US counties during the Great Recession
Authors: Scott Abrahams, Bulent Unel
Affiliations: Department of Economics Louisiana State University Baton Rouge Louisiana USA
Abstract: Abstract Exploiting variation in debt‐to‐income ratios across US counties at the onset of the Great Recession, we investigate the impact of debt exposure on suicide. We find that more indebted counties saw a significant rise in suicide rates, with effects double for men and triple among adults ages 40–64. These patterns align with financial responsibilities: men are primary borrowers on mortgages, and middle‐aged adults hold the most secured debt. The impact of debt on suicide behavior, with annual costs of several billion dollars, underscores the welfare implications of inflexible household debt instruments.

Title: From catastrophe to culture: The role of historical disasters in shaping long-term orientation
Authors: Meng Liu, Jun Wang, James B. Ang, Per G. Fredriksson

Title: Who drives inequality?
Authors: Domenico Moramarco, Olivier Sterck
Abstract: Which countries drive global inequality? Which states drive US inequality? We characterize the class of inequality measures that can answer these questions, permitting both an additive decomposition by subgroup and a multiplicative decomposition into within- and between-group components. Its central measure is simply the expected ratio of incomes between two randomly selected individuals. We show that global inequality fell since 1990, driven by declining disparities between countries. Inequality is primarily driven by large middle-income countries (India, China) and poor countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia). In the US, rising inequality is explained by widening gaps within states, while between-state inequality remains limited.

Title: Property rights and market frictions: Evidence from the universe of land dispute files in China
Authors: Jiong Zhu

Title: A decision support system to dynamically align supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across levels and time horizons
Authors: Pamela Danese, Marco Formentini, Pietro Romano, Marco Boem
Abstract: Supplier portfolio management is essential for organizations to achieve their strategic goals. However, there is a lack of decision support systems (DSSs) that can support purchasing managers simultaneously at the strategic, tactical and operational levels, while ensuring consistency of supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across different levels and time horizons. Existing DSSs based on purchasing portfolio models (PPMs) are static and typically address supplier or purchasing category segmentation and analysis at a single point in time. Following a design science paradigm, we specified, implemented, and evaluated NorthStar, a novel DSS for supplier portfolio management designed to align decisions and actions across levels and time horizons through a structured three-step procedure. Ex-ante and ex-post evaluations, conducted in both artificial and naturalistic settings, demonstrate the novelty, relevance, and utility of this artifact. Our study contributes to the theoretical debate at the intersection of supplier portfolio management, PPMs and DSSs, and sourcing strategy literatures. First, it demonstrates how a PPM-based DSS can align supplier portfolio decisions and actions across multiple levels, as well as across time horizons, while remaining consistent with category strategies. Second, it addresses the static nature of traditional PPMs by supporting a shift toward dynamic models that enable continuous monitoring and adaptation. Third, NorthStar operationalizes key theoretical constructs, such as dependence by suppliers, competition, and supplier portfolio complexity, translating them into measurable indicators within a structured decision process, thereby bridging theory and practice. Finally, it provides a flexible, data-driven procedure that enhances the applicability of portfolio approaches in real-world settings.

Title: Three horizon-specific drivers of gold prices with Iterated Dynamic Model Averaging
Authors: Sihan Chen, Shenggang Yang, Xiaomei Lan

Title: Do non-financial risks compound? Evidence from U.S. industry returns
Authors: Corrado Botta
Abstract: Non-financial risks affect asset prices individually, yet they are typically studied in isolation. Using 49 Fama–French industry portfolios over 1990–2026, we show that pairwise compound channels among geopolitical risk, climate policy uncertainty, and financial stress carry significant pricing power beyond individual exposures. Climate policy uncertainty emerges as the nexus variable: its interaction with financial conditions is the most consistent channel, surviving all standard error methods, sub-sample splits, and predetermined (lagged) financial conditions, with an effect roughly four times larger for carbon-intensive industries. A Wald test confirms the joint significance of the interactions while individual risks lack joint significance.

Title: Maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets
Authors: Øystein Foros
Abstract: We study maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets that share a common target retail price. A sufficiently small retailer margin can make the ceiling bind across markets, allowing common terms to implement this price. Two-part tariffs instead require the marginal wholesale price to align the retailer’s unconstrained optimal price exactly with the target. If the ceiling already binds, changes in market structure require no contractual recalibration. Apple’s use of list prices as de facto maximum resale prices, combined with discounts from those prices for independent resellers, illustrates a setting in which the mechanism may be relevant.

Title: Measuring the Sources of Taste-Based Discrimination Using List Experiments
Authors: Ariel Listo, Ercio A. Muñoz, Dario Sansone
Abstract: This paper examines how attitudes among supervisors, co-workers, and customers are related to discrimination against sexual minority individuals in the workplace. Participants from a large, nationally representative online sample in Chile took part in double list experiments  which reduce social desirability bias when eliciting views on sensitive topics  followed by direct questions on attitudes toward sexual minority individuals. The findings reveal a discrepancy between reported and actual levels of comfort with gay individuals in the labor market. The respondents underreported their discomfort by 15-23 percentage points, with the largest bias and lowest comfort levels observed when they were asked about supervising gay employees. These attitudinal patterns were mirrored in incentivized donation behavior: individuals who chose not to donate any amount from a lottery to a local LGBTQ-related nonprofit reported lower comfort levels and exhibited greater misreporting. Finally, the respondents consistently underestimated the broader societal support for gay employees and co-workers.

Title: HELP-RL: Real-time policy optimization with hierarchical decoder for heterogeneous and stochastic disaster response logistics
Authors: Hadi Aghazadeh, Xin Wang
Abstract: Disaster response logistics plays a vital role in reducing existential risk in relief operations by ensuring that essential resources reach affected communities promptly during emergencies. Although its significance is widely recognized, existing studies tend to focus primarily on pre-disaster planning, leaving notable gaps in addressing the complex, dynamic, and unpredictable challenges of real-time disaster response. This paper introduces a new framework called HELP-RL ( Humanitarian Emergency Logistics Planning with Reinforcement Learning ) to address these challenges, which are grouped into three main categories: heterogeneous fleet types, diverse demand types, and stochastic travel times. Together, these reflect the real-world complexities of disaster response logistics, all of which require real-time management. The HELP-RL framework incorporates a unique hierarchical decoder to manage the intricate action space, paired with an efficiently designed attention-based policy optimizer using the REINFORCE algorithm. This fully integrated model is built to adapt dynamically to changing disaster conditions, providing reliable and real-time solutions. To assess its performance, we tested the framework using both synthetic and real-world data from wildfire response logistics, drawing on actual data to replicate realistic scenarios. The findings show that HELP-RL produces adaptable and optimal policies that effectively handle rapid changes, surpassing other reinforcement learning approaches in terms of both efficiency and practical applicability.

Title: On disperse generalized linear models
Authors: Emilio Carrizosa, Renato De Leone, Marica Magagnini
Abstract: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) are a key tool in Explainable Machine Learning, since they provide an easy-to-understand explanation of their coefficients and the impact of the different features in predictions. However, not all accurate GLMs may be equally appealing due to presence of secondary objectives such as sparsity or other measurement costs. For this reason, several methods have been proposed in the literature to address the multiobjective problem of joint optimization of accuracy and other secondary criteria, sparsity being the most popular objective if explainability is pursued. In this work we explore how different GLMs with good accuracy can be. We consider a biobjective P -Dispersion Problem, in which P models are sought jointly maximizing an overall accuracy measure as well as a dispersion measure. Several metrics are used to measure dispersion, such as a function of the distance between their parameters or the set of features used to predict. Moreover, different scenarios for the feasible region are considered, e.g., whether the P models are to be chosen from, or added to, a list of pre-selected GLMs. All these variants are expressed as biobjective nonlinear mixed integer optimization problems. Numerical tests are also presented, showing the effectiveness and the relevance of the proposed methodology.

Title: The regional economic impact of weather shocks: Evidence from Portugal
Authors: Dhruv Akshay Pandit, Paulo M.M. Rodrigues, João Seixo
Abstract: Weather extremes shape short-run economic activity through both market and nonmarket channels, yet evidence on local consumer-side activity remains limited. Using a municipality-level panel of Portuguese data (2010–2021), we estimate panel VAR and local-projection responses to weather shocks of point-of-sale purchases (a measure of merchant-location transaction activity, not resident household consumption), together with unemployment and house prices. Our central methodological finding is that hourly rather than daily measurement of rainfall variability raises the estimated semi-elasticities by an order of magnitude, suggesting that the existing climate-economy literature systematically understates the importance of high-intensity rainfall. Substantively, the local-projection responses indicate that hourly rainfall volatility raises purchases on impact and reverses the following quarter, consistent with intertemporal reallocation; temperature variability generates a sharp positive impact effect followed by a contraction; and high fire-danger days raise contemporaneous purchases. Unemployment and house prices follow the same patterns more weakly. Regional heterogeneity is substantial, the Lisbon Metropolitan Area and the Algarve sometimes display effects opposite in sign to those in the North.
