Title: Beggars cannot be choosers: Labor market tightness, hiring standards, wages, and hiring costs
Authors: Carolin Linckh, Samuel Muehlemann, Harald Pfeifer
Abstract: This study analyzes how hiring standards, entry wages, and hiring costs are associated with labor market tightness. Using unique linked employer-employee data for small- and medium-sized firms in Germany, we find that pre-match search costs represent only 16 percent of total hiring expenditures, while post-match costs account for the remaining 84 percent. Instrumental variable regressions show no evidence that tighter labor markets are associated with higher entry wages. Instead, we find differences along two non-wage dimensions. First, firms hire workers whose general ability is lower relative to their existing workforce. Second, firms incur higher post-match hiring costs for these hires. A one standard deviation increase in labor market tightness is associated with a 0.1 standard deviation decrease in hiring standards, an 11 percent longer adaptation period, and 15 percent higher informal training hours for new hires. These findings suggest that, in tight labor markets, variation in hiring outcomes is reflected more strongly in hiring standards and post-hire training investments than in entry wages.

Title: Motherhood timing and the child penalty
Authors: Anikó Bíró, Steven Dieterle, Andreas Steinhauer
Abstract: Abstract Age at first birth has increased over time, which is likely to create many benefits in the labour market. Applying a number of alternative estimation approaches to administrative data from Austria, we estimate small to moderate effects of delaying motherhood on earnings, employment, and attachment to pre-birth firms in the medium run. However, even the largest of these effects are small relative to the average age effects, implying that delay leads to only small changes in child penalties. Much of the career return to later first birth comes from delaying the child penalty rather than changing how careers respond to children.

Title: A hybrid model proposal and an application for solving the problem of solid waste collection
Authors: İzzettin Hakan Karaçizmeli, Serkan Kaya
Abstract: The increasing amount of municipal household solid waste generated due to population growth and rising consumption has become a major environmental and economic problem for local governments. Waste collection and transportation activities constitute a significant portion of municipal solid waste management costs and are commonly formulated as vehicle routing problems. This study addresses a real-world municipal household solid waste collection problem involving 280 waste container locations in the Veysel Karani neighbourhood of Şanlıurfa, Türkiye. To solve the problem, a hybrid particle swarm optimisation algorithm combining particle swarm optimisation and local search strategies is proposed. The performance of the proposed algorithm was compared with linear programming, ArcGIS, real-life routing results, and previously developed metaheuristic approaches in the literature. The experimental results demonstrated that the proposed algorithm produced superior results, particularly for medium- and large-sized problem sets. Overall, the proposed method achieved 7.81% improvement over the linear programming model, 5.23% over the ArcGIS method, 33.46% over actual operational routes, and 0.24% over the improved hybrid firefly and particle swarm optimisation algorithm. In addition, statistical analyses based on Friedman and Wilcoxon tests confirmed that the proposed algorithm significantly outperformed the competing methods. The findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide an effective and practical solution for real-world municipal household solid waste collection problems.

Title: Integrating internal and external attributes in clustering: a goal programming-data envelopment analysis model
Authors: Hashem Omrani
Abstract: Conventional clustering methods group objects based on similarities in external data, often overlooking internal characteristics of decision-making units (DMUs), such as their production functions. In contrast, data envelopment analysis (DEA), a data-oriented nonparametric methodology, enables clustering based on the production frontier. However, traditional DEA models do not account for the distance between DMUs, and the resulting clusters are often non-unique, allowing a DMU to be assigned to multiple clusters. To address both internal and external characteristics, this paper proposes a goal programming–DEA (GP-DEA) model that clusters DMUs using both the production function and the distances between them. First, an envelopment form of the DEA model is applied to identify the initial clusters. Then, a GP-DEA model is used to determine a set of common weights for the input and output variables of the DMUs within each cluster. In each cluster, the efficiency scores of DMUs are recalculated using the new common weights. If the new efficiency of a DMU does not match the efficiency generated by the traditional DEA model, the DMU is removed from the cluster. In addition, a DMU initially assigned to multiple clusters is ultimately allocated to the cluster where its efficiency score remains unchanged. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we present numerical examples and analyze a case study of 288 hospitals using the proposed GP-DEA model.

Title: Social Effects of the Vote of the Majority: An Experiment on the Brexit‐Vote
Authors: Fernanda Leite Lopez de Leon, Markus Bindemann
Affiliations: School of Economics, Politics and International Relations University of Kent Canterbury UK; School of Psychology University of Kent Canterbury UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT The 2016 EU referendum result was widely perceived as a statement against immigration. This paper investigates whether information about majority voting outcomes influences attitudes towards immigrants. Using a survey experiment conducted in England in 2017–2018, we randomly exposed participants to truthful information indicating that local constituencies had predominantly voted either to Leave or to Remain in the 2016 EU referendum. The intervention substantially shifted beliefs about local Brexit vote shares. Although we find no statistically significant effects on most individual survey questions, exposure to a Leave‐majority signal leads to more restrictive immigration policy preferences relative to exposure to a Remain‐majority signal. Effects are concentrated among participants for whom the information was politically dissonant or unexpected. Overall, the pattern of results is consistent with a conformity mechanism operating through perceived majority views, suggesting that referenda may continue to shape expressed policy preferences beyond their immediate aftermath.

Title: Welfare implications of no net loss policies with heterogeneous cultural ecosystem services
Authors: Cathrine Hagem
Abstract: No net loss (NNL) targets for nature are increasingly implemented at both national and subnational levels. While these policies are typically framed in terms of area or biophysical equivalence, they may overlook heterogeneity in the cultural ecosystem service (CES) values associated with undeveloped land. This paper develops a parsimonious economic model to analyze the welfare implications of alternative NNL policy designs when CES values differ across municipalities. We distinguish between local CES values, such as recreational and amenity benefits accruing to nearby populations, and a national CES value associated with the existence of undeveloped nature. We compare unilateral and cooperative municipal policies and examine the performance of taxes and subsidies versus offset markets under area-based and CES value-based NNL targets. We show that area-based NNL policies are generally welfare suboptimal in the presence of heterogeneous local CES values, even when implemented cost-effectively through offset markets. By contrast, NNL targets defined in CES value terms can achieve constrained welfare optima using appropriately designed fiscal instruments or ambient permit markets. Although inter-municipal cooperation reduces aggregate costs, distributional effects may prevent mutually beneficial outcomes without side payments. Numerical illustrations based on Norwegian data support the analytical results and highlight implications for subnational and national offset policy design.

Title: The appearance of democracy: How conditional payments reshape behavior among local leaders
Authors: Ivo Steimanis, Esther Blanco, Björn Vollan
Abstract: Monetary incentives are widely considered to promote democratic practices in local governance. We test this proposition by providing causal evidence from a lab-in-the-field experiment with local leaders (n=64) and their constituents (n=384) in rural Namibia's hybrid governance setting. Using a within-subject design, we introduced conditional payments to leaders for allowing constituents to vote on how to distribute a collective fund. A majority of leaders (64%) chose a democratic rule at baseline, and the payments did not significantly increase this share. The incentives caused a significant reduction in openly autocratic behavior, primarily through a shift toward a pseudo-democratic practice of appearing democratic while retaining unilateral decision-making. This reveals unintended consequences of the conditional incentives, fostering symbolic compliance where leaders appear democratic while retaining control. Exploratory analysis shows payments "crowd out" democracy among initially democratic leaders but "crowd in" pseudo-democracy among autocratic leaders, moderated by governing motivations. Our findings illustrate that conditional payments can fail to foster genuine democracy and caution against their prescriptive use in complex governance environments.

Title: Enhancing port channel logistics safety: An asynchronous distributed DRL approach for waterborne ASVs trajectory tracking under dynamic disturbances
Authors: Chongwei Gong, Zhen Tian, Yusheng Zhou
Abstract: Port channel safety is essential for reliable vessel movements and efficient logistics operations in intelligent ports. Waterborne ASVs can support inspection, monitoring, and auxiliary transportation in restricted port waters, but their deployment requires accurate trajectory tracking to avoid additional port-channel navigational safety risks. However, reliable ASV tracking remains challenging under dynamic disturbances and strict ship-to-shore communication constraints. This study proposes an Asynchronous Distributed Deep Reinforcement Learning (AD-DRL) control scheme for robust ASV trajectory tracking under dynamic marine disturbances. Unlike traditional centralized training, the proposed framework enables distributed ASVs to collaboratively update policies by exchanging model gradients rather than raw sensor data, thereby reducing communication requirements. To improve decision-making in dynamic waters, a gated hybrid attention mechanism is integrated into the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) architecture. This mechanism helps the agent capture spatiotemporal disturbance features and delayed vessel responses caused by hydrodynamic lag. Moreover, an ERA5-informed data-driven simulation environment is constructed using real-world ocean current, wind, and wave data to train and evaluate the controller. Experiments across five representative international ports show that the proposed method achieves lower tracking errors and higher success rates than baseline methods under varying environmental disturbances. Additional safety-corridor analysis further confirms its ability to maintain reliable trajectory execution in port channels. These results demonstrate the robustness and practical relevance of AD-DRL, providing technical support for safer and more reliable ASV operations in intelligent port logistics scenarios.

Title: Is irregular migration responsive to recent German asylum policy adjustments?
Authors: Bernd Beber, Cara Ebert, Maximiliane Sievert
Abstract: We investigate the extent to which asylum policies that aim to deter individuals from migrating irregularly in fact do so. We specifically consider effects of Germany’s 2023 asylum policy adjustments, which include accelerated asylum decision processes, the prospect of asylum processing outside of Europe, the introduction of a payment card to replace cash benefits, and an extended waiting period for native-level benefits. To estimate the effects of these policy measures on irregular migration intent, we implement a conjoint experiment with 989 men aged 18–40 in four cities in Senegal, a country where irregular migration to Europe is highly salient. Offshoring the asylum process substantially lowers irregular migration intentions, and extending the waiting time for native-level benefits only has a small effect on intent. Neither reducing asylum processing times nor replacing cash benefits with a payment card alters intentions. Our study does not resolve political and normative questions concerning these policies.

Title: Fickle fossils: Economic growth, coal, and the European oil invasion, 1900–2015
Authors: Miriam Fritzsche, Nikolaus Wolf
Abstract: Fossil fuels have shaped the European economy since the industrial revolution. We use new long-run panel data to analyse the effect of both, coal and oil on economic growth between 1900 and 2015, exploiting variation at the level of European NUTS2 and NUTS3 regions. We show that the reversal of fortune of coal regions resulted from the second energy transition. Specifically, an “oil invasion” in the early 1960s turned regional coal abundance from a blessing into a curse. Human capital accumulation contributed to this reversal of fortune and fully explains the negative effects until today. Moreover, we find substantial heterogeneity between former coal regions that is in line with Glaeser’s “reinvention hypothesis”: regions with a higher skill-level adjusted much better to the decline of coal. In particular, we show that coal regions with a higher urban density before 1800 were much more resilient than others.

Title: The Curvilinear Impact of Environmental Sustainability Strategies on Cost and Profit Growth: The Moderating Influence of Operations, R&D, and Logistics Capabilities
Authors: Siavash Rashidi‐Sabet, Sreedhar Madhavaram
Affiliations: Department of MIS, Marketing, and Analytics| Saunders College of Business, Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester New York USA; Department of Marketing and Supply Chain Management| Jerry S. Rawls College of Business Administration, Texas Tech University Lubbock Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Research linking environmental sustainability efforts and firm performance provides equivocal evidence of negative, neutral, or positive effects. Drawing on myopic management theory, this research develops and tests a time‐contingent, nonlinear account of how corporate environmental sustainability performance shapes cost growth and profit growth. This research conceptualizes environmental sustainability initiatives as requiring up‐front process redesign and coordination investments that elevate short‐run cost growth and compress profitability, but yield delayed benefits as implementation stabilizes and learning accumulates. This research further examines how three core functional capabilities relevant to logistics and supply chain execution—operations capability, R&D capability, and logistics capability—condition these curvilinear trajectories. Analyses of data from 498 U.S. public firms over 2012–2024 show an inverted U‐shaped relationship between environmental sustainability performance and cost growth and a U‐shaped relationship with profit growth, with both relationships evolving over time. Analyses indicate that core functional capabilities meaningfully condition these curvilinear relationships, shaping the magnitude and timing of sustainability‐related cost escalation and profitability improvement. The findings position sustainability as a staged logistics and supply chain implementation challenge and indicate that investing in logistics execution effectiveness and innovation scaling helps firms manage transition frictions and translate sustainability initiatives into more stable long‐horizon performance improvements.

Title: The costs of access: Freeway disamenities across US cities
Authors: Jeffrey Brinkman, Jeffrey Lin

Title: When brands go live: AI host or profit-popularity driven influencer?
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Xingyun Yue, Fanzhuo Zeng, Nan Zhang
Affiliations: South China University of Technology; University of Southampton
Abstract: Livestreaming sales (LSS) has become one of the fastest-growing formats in digital commerce, yet rising commission rates render influencer-led livestreaming increasingly costly. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a promising alternative: AI-powered virtual hosts that engage consumers and promote products without commission payments, albeit with lower interactional efficiency. This paper examines the brand's strategic choice between influencer-led and AI-hosted LSS. We develop an analytical model involving a brand and a dual-purpose influencer who values both commission and popularity-related benefits such as follower-base expansion. Our analysis uncovers two opposing mechanisms shaping how cost dynamics affect livestreaming choices. The influencer interactional-compensation effect captures the influencer's tendency to raise interactional richness as product cost increases, thereby helping stabilise demand. In contrast, the AI price-stabilisation effect results in lower interactional investment but more stable pricing. We show that when the influencer cares only about commission earnings, AI hosting is optimal only for low-cost products. If the influencer is profit-popularity driven, however, AI hosting may remain profitable for mid-to-high-cost products when AI is inefficient and popularity incentive is strong. Our results highlight the importance of tailoring livestreaming mode with product cost structure and the moderating role of the influencer's profit-popularity motivation.

Title: Resource allocation and patient care: a two-stage network-DEA model for optimising rural hospital operations
Authors: Guilherme P. Afonso, Dinesh R. Pai, José Rui Figueira, Diogo Filipe Cunha Ferreira
Affiliations: CERIS, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa; Penn State Harrisburg; CEGIST, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa
Abstract: We propose an evaluation framework to enhance U.S. rural hospital efficiency and sustainability amid rising costs and staffing shortages. Moving beyond ‘black-box’ evaluations, we utilise a two-stage Network-Data Envelopment Analysis (N-DEA) Slack-Based Measure model - Resource Allocation and Patient Care Delivery – to analyse internal inefficiencies. To ensure validity, 57 rural hospitals were segmented by size. To capture performance evolution, we integrate the Hicks-Moorsteen Productivity Index to evaluate annual Total Factor Productivity (TFP) shifts. We model hospitals as production systems converting resources into health outcomes. Applied to a 2018–2023 dataset, the model reveals that Patient Care Delivery consistently outperforms Resource Allocation. Longitudinal analysis indicates that while 48 of 57 hospitals recorded net TFP increases, volatility persists, particularly among small and medium facilities. This suggests performance gains are achievable by addressing Resource Allocation bottlenecks. Slack analysis reveals divergent profiles: small hospitals frequently operate with zero slack, whereas the broader sample shows 20% average excess for physicians and certified nurse practitioners. Scenario testing confirms modest reductions (25%) in these roles would enhance efficiency by 1.8%. Conversely, we recommend protecting registered nurse staffing due to minimal slack (6%), as potential efficiency gains are outweighed by patient care risks. This study offers data-driven insights for healthcare decision-makers.

Title: A scheduling problem in a reconfigurable manufacturing system with stochastic worker availability: a hybrid L-shaped decomposition method
Authors: Hessam Bakhshi-Khaniki, Reza Tavakkoli-Moghaddam, Zdenek Hanzalek, Behdin Vahedi-Nouri
Affiliations: University of Tehran; Istinye University; Czech Institute of Informatics Robotics and Cybernetics, Czech Technical University in Prague
Abstract: Modern manufacturing faces growing challenges from market volatility, resource uncertainty, and the need for quick adaptation. Reconfigurable Manufacturing Systems (RMSs) offer a flexible adaptable solution; however, scheduling becomes more complex when worker availability is uncertain. Workers in RMSs represent limited and mobile resources, whose uncertain availability can severely disrupt production efficiency. This paper investigates the non-identical parallel machine scheduling problem in an RMS under stochastic worker availability. To tackle this complex optimisation problem, a two-stage stochastic programming model is developed. In the first stage, job-to-machine assignments are determined as here-and-now decisions. The second stage involves optimising job sequencing, machine configurations, and worker assignments after the worker availability scenarios are revealed. To solve this problem, a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and an L-shaped Decomposition (LD) method are developed to minimise the expected makespan. To enhance solution efficiency, a novel CP-LD is proposed, where the master problem uses MILP while subproblems employ Constraint Programming (CP). Computational results show that the proposed CP-LD method outperforms the MILP and LD methods in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. The sensitivity analysis provides insights into the impact of various system parameters on the expected makespan performance, highlighting the critical importance of workforce management.

Title: A hybrid solution approach for the joint optimisation of skeleton cut line layout and cutting path planning
Authors: Yuanpeng Lai, Shaowen Yao, Meng Tian, Hao Zhang, Congyi Wang, Jiewu Leng, Qiang Liu
Affiliations: Guangdong University of Technology; CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding Company Limited
Abstract: In CNC cutting scenarios such as large-scale shipbuilding, net-like scrap skeletons formed by cutting often lead to difficulties in separating nested parts, and their dimensions frequently exceed the handling limits of automated equipment or scrap containers, thus necessitating further segmentation. Existing ‘skeleton cut line’ (SCL) processes heavily rely on manual experience, making it difficult to balance scrap disposal requirements and processing efficiency. To address this, we propose the Joint Optimisation Problem of Skeleton Cut Line Layout and Cutting Path Planning, aiming to synergistically determine the SCL layout, cutting sequence, and entry points to minimise total processing costs under process constraints. We construct a mixed-integer linear programming model that integrates the Extended Precedence-Constrained Generalised Travelling Salesman Problem with the Weighted Set Covering Problem, and propose a two-stage heuristic hybrid solution approach of ‘geometry generation–dynamic optimisation’. The first stage constructs a finite high-quality candidate SCL set via geometric rules; the second employs a hybrid heuristic integrating Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search, Simulated Annealing, and Local Search for efficient joint dynamic optimisation. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world industrial instances verify the model accuracy and demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in solution quality, efficiency, and robustness, confirming its practical applicability.

Title: Profit-oriented dynamic scheduling for disassembly flexible job shops: dealing with structural uncertainty and operation skipping
Authors: Zengyu Kuang, Hui Xie, Yinghui Ren, Xiaojun Zhuo, Minghao Shi
Affiliations: Hunan University; Changsha Research Institute of Mining and Metallurgy Co Ltd
Abstract: Disassembly scheduling for End-of-Life (EOL) products, particularly EV batteries, exhibits dynamic structural uncertainty and physical degradation characteristics. However, existing scheduling models are predominantly static and fail to fully capture the distinctive stochastic features and operation skipping patterns of such disassembly systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the process as a Markov Decision Process and propose a Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (H-MADRL) framework. To enhance practical applicability, a Hierarchical State Embedding module acts as a digital perception layer to quantify physical risks. Meanwhile, a Physics-Informed Dual-Agent mechanism coordinates task-machine assignments, and a Constraint-Compliant Masking layer ensures strict adherence to Standard Operating Procedures. Averaged over multiple independent runs, the framework achieves a 45.6% increase in profit rate and a 16.9% reduction in makespan compared to standard reinforcement learning and heuristic baselines. Ultimately, this approach secures shop-floor adaptability and significantly advances managerial precision in balancing economic density with operational throughput under stochastic constraints.

Title: A fix-and-relax matheuristic method for lot-sizing and scheduling problem in a dairy industry
Authors: Parisa Pourabdollah, Saeed Emami, Ebrahim Asadi-Gangraj
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Babol Noshiravani University of Technology
Abstract: The lot-sizing and scheduling problem (LSP) focuses on determining the production quantities and the sequence of production activities, simultaneously. This article addresses the LSP in a flexible flow shop environment within the real-world dairy industry in Iran. We consider perishability, which is a common issue in the food industry, as well as cleaning in place (CIP) of the machines. The problem can be described as multi-product, multi-level, multi-period, with sequence-dependent setup and CIP time. To maximise profits, we present a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that subtracts total revenue from the total cost, including tardiness, inventory holding, sequence-dependent setup, CIP, and disposal of perished products costs. Due to the NP-hardness of this problem, we propose a fix-and-relax (F&R) matheuristic method to solve it. The numerical experiments on randomly generated instances with up to 40 products on the proposed model show that while the exact MILP model becomes computationally intractable for large-scale instances, the proposed F&R method is able to generate high-quality feasible solutions within reasonable computation times.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Operationalizing circular supply chains through integrating product development and supply chain design: a multi-phase framework grounded in multiple case studies
Authors: Sobhan Mostafayi Darmian, Sotirios Panagou, Fabio Sgarbossa
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, NTNU
Abstract: Manufacturing firms seeking to implement circular economy strategies often face a practical challenge in translating R-imperatives into coordinated decisions on product development and supply chain design. Although prior studies and conceptual frameworks have highlighted the importance of integrating these domains, there is limited guidance on how to operationalise such integration in practice. In response, this study develops a three-phase operationalisation framework for integrating R-imperatives, product development, and supply chain design. The framework comprises an As-Is phase, which identifies the current product and supply chain configuration and assesses the existing level of integration, a To-Be phase, which identifies feasible R-imperatives and the redesign requirements they imply, and a To-Do phase, which identifies implementation challenges, capability gaps, and action priorities. The framework is built on the existing knowledge in the literature and empirically grounded through multiple case studies of Norwegian manufacturing companies. The findings show that the feasibility of R-imperatives depends strongly on product architecture, reverse logistics capabilities, and the synchronisation between product redesign and supply chain adaptation. The study contributes by moving beyond conceptual recognition of integration towards a practical framework that supports design for circularity in industrial settings.

Title: Universalization and the origins of fiscal capacity
Authors: Esteban Muñoz-Sobrado
Abstract: This paper proposes a model of tax compliance and fiscal capacity grounded in universalization reasoning. Citizens partially internalize the consequences of concealment by imagining a world in which everyone acted similarly, linking their compliance decisions to the perceived effectiveness of public spending. A selfish elite chooses between public goods and private rents, taking compliance as given. In equilibrium, citizens' moral internalization expands the feasible tax base and induces elites to allocate resources toward provision rather than appropriation. When the value of public spending is uncertain, morality enables credible reform: high-value elites can signal their type through provision, prompting citizens to increase compliance and raising fiscal capacity within the same period. The analysis thus identifies a moral channel through which states may escape low-capacity traps even under weak institutions.

Title: Editorial Board
Evidence of firm-level pollution leakage resulting from China's 2013 Clean Air Plan
Authors: Chang Liu, Jingrong Wang, David M. Reiner
Abstract: Spatially differentiated environmental regulation can induce pollution leakage through intra-firm relocation of pollution-intensive activities to less-regulated regions. This mechanism remains underexplored, especially in developing countries, where data limitations make intra-firm relocation difficult to measure and existing investment-based proxies often miss expansions within existing subsidiaries. Using manually collected subsidiary-level investment data for 411 listed pollution-intensive firms in China and a difference-in-differences framework, we examine whether regionally differentiated regulation under the 2013 Clean Air Plan led to intra-firm investment reallocation consistent with production relocation and potential domestic pollution leakage. We find that regulated firms increased pollution-related investment in subsidiaries located in less-regulated areas following the policy, accompanied by declines in parent-firm output and rising PM₂.₅ concentrations around subsidiary locations. Adjustment patterns differ across regions: firms in the three key regions centered on Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou reallocate investment from eastern regulated areas to distant western regions, mainly through new subsidiary entry, whereas firms in ten other major city clusters mainly expand existing subsidiaries located nearby. Reallocated investment is disproportionately directed toward regions with stronger agglomeration economies and transportation advantages rather than environmentally fragile areas. These findings suggest that investment flows offer a valuable lens for detecting potential pollution leakage and that unintended east-to-west transfers may undermine environmental gains, highlighting the need for stronger disclosure requirements and targeted pollution-control policies in recipient regions.

Title: Optimal climate and monetary–fiscal policies in a climate-DSGE framework
Authors: Lorenzo Forni, Mehrab Kiarsi
Abstract: This paper studies the optimal design of climate, fiscal, and monetary policies in response to climate-specific shocks within a climate-DSGE framework. We show that carbon taxes significantly mitigate the effects of climate shocks on output, consumption, and welfare, while optimal monetary policy is largely unaffected and fiscal policy adjusts via lower labor taxes. Extending the model with a richer climate module and abatement costs, we find that the assumed damage function is crucial: under a standard quadratic specification, climate policy has little effect on conventional macroeconomic shocks, but a highly convex, Weitzman-type damage function makes carbon taxation materially relevant. Accounting for climate fiscal outlays further raises optimal abatement and reduces emissions. Our results highlight the importance of integrating both macroeconomic and environmental considerations when designing policy.

Title: Roadside native species seeding practices of Midwestern US departments of transportation
Authors: Wesley J. Bollinger, Rabin Bhattarai, Jeffrey W. Matthews
Abstract: To counteract environmental problems associated with road construction and maintenance, road agencies have developed vegetation management plans that incorporate native seeding. We reviewed the specifications manuals from the Departments of Transportation of eight US states to synthesize information on native plant species used, seed mixes, site preparation, seeding methods, and maintenance to provide recommendations for roadside vegetation management. Manuals varied among states in terms of the species composition and functional diversity of plants listed for use. Individual mixes included an average of 14 native species, although some had as few as 3, and many lacked functional diversity or early blooming forbs that would benefit pollinators. We identified several early-blooming, low-cost, conservative plant species that could be incorporated into seed mixes. Compared to other states, Minnesota listed more native species and seed mixes, and provided detailed specifications for seeding, establishment, and maintenance, aligning well with recommendations based on ecological restoration research.

Title: The Wheel of Satisfaction: Cyclists’ perceptions and environmental Mindsets

Title: Kuhn’s theorem for games of the extensive form with unawareness
Authors: Ki Vin Foo, Burkhard C. Schipper
Abstract: We extend Kuhn's Theorem to games of the extensive form with unawareness. We prove that if a game of the extensive form with unawareness has perfect recall, then for each mixed strategy there is an equivalent behavior strategy. We show that the converse does not hold under unawareness without restricting the evolution of the player's awareness to constant awareness along paths of play. Both directions of Kuhn's Theorem for games of the extensive form with unawareness require a condition complementary to perfect recall that rules out falsely believing in some events when the player is unaware of the actual past events.

Title: Note on abundance or scarcity for the Wicksellian production function, or, When does an AC-curve become U-shaped?
Authors: Robert W. Grubbström
Abstract: This note attempts to find conditions for the average cost curve to have a U-shape for problems applying the Wicksellian production function (most often called the Cobb-Douglas function ) in combination with limits in the supplies of production factors. This function enables explicit solutions to be found. On the road towards conclusions, it was found that each factor could be ranked conveniently by an abundance index defined as its factor price, multiplied by its limit amount, and divided by the value of its weight parameter. This enables an ordered sequence of critical output volumes to be defined and found, at which levels the factor amounts meet their available limits, respectively. It is demonstrated that in order for an AC -curve to have a U-shape, there must be at least one production factor with limited supplies, and that the remaining non-limited factors have weights such that their sum complies with diminishing returns to scale (sum of weights being less than unity). A reasoning on the effect that scarcity has on fixed costs and thereby on competition rounds off this note.

Title: Joint optimization of fleet size and operating speed for service planning in oversaturated urban rail transit networks
Authors: Siyu Zhuo, Xiaoning Zhu, Pan Shang, Zhengke Liu, Feixiong Liao
Abstract: Oversaturated operations have become increasingly common in urban rail transit (URT) systems, where peak-period passenger demand often exceeds available service capacity. This demand–capacity imbalance leads to platform queues, in-train crowding, and denied boarding, making service planning particularly challenging when fleet resources are limited. To address the coupled supply–demand interactions, this study proposes a novel Behavior–Energy-Adaptive Service planning (BEAS) framework for network-wide URT service planning, in which fleet allocation and line-level operating speed are jointly optimized while passengers’ adaptive route choices are explicitly modeled. An integrated nonlinear integer programming model is developed to link fleet–speed service-plan decisions, subject to fleet budget limits and speed-dependent traction energy costs, with passenger assignment and path-size logit (PSL)-based route choice in a capacity-constrained space–time network. By enforcing train capacity and first-in-first-out (FIFO) boarding, the model reproduces platform queueing and denied boarding, and captures how the resulting time-dependent travel costs drive adaptive rerouting under oversaturated conditions. To solve the resulting large-scale coupled problem, a decomposition-based iterative algorithm is developed, in which the demand-side subproblem simulates individual passenger assignment under time-dependent costs and the supply-side subproblem optimizes fleet and speed decisions through an incremental approximation that yields a tractable multiple-choice knapsack structure. Numerical experiments on both a small illustrative network and a large-scale Beijing metro network demonstrate the computational efficiency, scalability, and practical value of the proposed framework. The results show that coordinated fleet–speed service planning can substantially reduce waiting time and left-behind passengers under resource constraints, while supporting passenger-oriented, operator-oriented, and balanced service planning.

Title: Editorial Board
Building resilience amidst a crisis: An automaker’s procurement journey to secure semiconductor supply
Authors: José Augusto Campos Garcia, Ala Arvidsson, Patrik Jonsson
Abstract: SummaryEvents such as the semiconductors shortage crisis of 2020 and 2023 caused severe shortages across different industries. This specific crisis forced automakers to take several measures to secure supplies and highlighted the need for resilience. With procurement as the core function to manage supply, this study investigates how procurement contributes to building supply chain resilience during high-impact and long-lasting disruptions. Drawing on the adaptive cycle perspective of resilience, we investigate how procurement supports persistence, adaptation, and transformation in response to disruption. Using in-depth data from a case of a commercial vehicle Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM), we follow the procurement measures across the phases of the semiconductor crisis. The findings show that procurement not only enables operational continuity through internal coordination and external information flows, but also facilitates strategic adaptation by reconfiguring processes and relationships. Most notably, procurement drives transformation of a firm’s supply chain management by institutionalizing new roles internally and redefining its role in the supply network. A conceptual framework is proposed that links procurement to changes in supply chain potential and connectedness, offering new insights into procurement’s role for resilience across the adaptive cycle.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: Using optimization and AI for large-scale stochastic resource planning
Authors: Hector G. de Alba, Haitao Li, Andres Tellez-Crespo, Cipriano Arturo Santos, Jose Emmanuel Gomez-Rocha, Marcos C. Vargas, Victor A. Regueira, Lyle Ramshaw, Adrian Ramirez-Nafarrate
Abstract: Resource planning plays an important role in matching resources with projects and jobs with multiple attributes. Motivated by real world applications at professional service organizations (PSOs), we coin and study the stochastic resource planning (SRP) problem with both the demand- and supply-side uncertainties due to uncertain bidding outcome and attrition. A two-stage stochastic programming model is developed for the SRP, which is shown to have properties for the model to be transformed to a polynomially solvable minimum cost matching problem. This makes it possible to solve large-scale SRP instances to optimality efficiently. In addition, we develop advanced machine learning techniques to feed the proposed model with the parameters needed, such as the matching score. We present a use case at a PSO for its IT recruiting application. Real life data of resumes and job descriptions from career websites are collected and applied to estimate the matching scores. Comparing with the expected value approach, our SRP solution achieves significantly better performance metrics of staffing cost, resource utilization and job fulfillment.

Title: Non‐Regular Distributions, Virtual Values and Monopoly Problems
Authors: Paolo Morganti
Affiliations: Facultad de Ciencias Económicas y Empresariales Universidad Panamericana Mexico City Mexico
Abstract: ABSTRACT We revisit the standard regularity assumption used to ensure uniqueness of the optimal price in monopoly models, namely that the Virtual Value (VV) function is monotone. This condition is typically imposed through strong distributional assumptions, such as log‐concavity, that restrict the model's flexibility and implicitly discipline the sign of comparative statics. We show that these assumptions can be relaxed without compromising tractability or uniqueness. Our main contribution is to introduce ‐Regularity, a weaker condition that requires monotonicity of the VV only beyond the threshold where marginal revenue becomes nonnegative. We demonstrate that many common non‐regular, unimodal distributions satisfy this local condition. This shift in focus allows standard first‐order methods to remain valid, and it enlarges the set of tractable demand primitives in applied IO. As an implication, when hazard rates are not monotone over the relevant pricing range, comparative statics need not follow the direction imposed by log‐concavity. The framework also reduces the need for ironing when modeling with heavy‐tailed demand.

Title: Top-Two Thompson Sampling for Contextual Selection Problems
Authors: Xinbo Shi, Yijie Peng, Gongbo Zhang
Affiliations: Department of Management Science and Information Systems, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Department of AI for Management, School of Management and Engineering, School of Computer Science, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210008, China; and Wuhan Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University, Wuhan 100080, China; and Xiangjiang Laboratory, Changsha 410205, China; School of Economics and Management, Beihang University, Beijing 100191, China
Abstract: We aim to efficiently allocate a fixed simulation budget to identify the best designs for each context among a finite number of contexts. The performance of each design in a context is measured by an identifiable statistical characteristic, possibly with the existence of nuisance parameters. In a Bayesian framework, we extend the top-two Thompson sampling method designed for selecting the best design in a single context to the contextual selection problems, leading to an efficient sampling policy that simultaneously allocates simulation samples to both contexts and designs. To demonstrate the asymptotic optimality of the proposed sampling policy, we establish a posterior large deviations principle for the focal model, characterizing the exponential convergence rate of the posterior distribution for a broad range of identifiable sampling distribution families. The proposed sampling policy is then proved to be consistent and asymptotically satisfies a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality. We also discuss extending the proposed sampling policy to solve the contextual top-[Formula: see text] problems and show that a necessary condition for optimality is asymptotically attained. Numerical experiments demonstrate the good finite-sample performance of the proposed sampling policy. Title: Technology-resource interaction innovation decisions in small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprise alliances: A dynamic biform game model
Authors: Xiaowei Ma, Weimin Ma
Abstract: Manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often struggle with innovation because of resource and technology constraints. To address this challenge, in this study, a dynamic biform game model is constructed to analyse the formation and stabilization mechanisms of innovation alliances. A synergy hub that employs a dual-cost allocation strategy and greedy matching algorithm is a key model component. In each cycle, firms first determine their technological investments noncooperatively on the basis of the expected returns. The synergy hub then prioritizes matching the most efficient resources within the alliance to the technologically weakest firms, while costs are allocated according to the principle of group incentive compatibility. Simulation results demonstrate that this mechanism significantly stimulates innovation among heterogeneous firms. Specifically, by accessing synergistically empowered resources, technology- catch up firms increase their technology capacity more than 40% faster than through independent innovation. Resource-dependent firms, provided that they activate the pathway from resource empowerment to technological advancement, may achieve up to a 30% rebound in utility. However, synergistic effects exhibit notable industry heterogeneity. The empirical analysis indicates that more than 76% of the innovation performance improvement within the alliance is attributable to increased resource efficiency. This effect is most pronounced in the pharmaceutical industry, whereas in process-driven sectors such as those involving chemicals, diminishing returns may lead to suboptimal outcomes. This study confirms that an innovation alliance embedded with an incentive-compatible allocation mechanism not only improves innovation performance through resource pooling but also promotes dynamic stability by reshaping innovation pressure. The findings provide a clear theoretical foundation and quantitative reference for SMEs in terms of selecting innovation pathways and for policymakers in terms of designing industrial collaboration platforms.

Title: The dismal theorem in a general equilibrium climate-economy model
Authors: Christoph Hambel, Frederick van der Ploeg
Abstract: We show that Weitzman (2009)’s dismal theorem resurfaces naturally within a dynamic asset pricing framework with temperature-related disaster risk. If the climate disaster loss distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, the risk-adjusted expected loss term diverges. Under unit elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS), this causes the social cost of carbon (SCC) to explode and the underlying optimization problem to have no finite solution so that the dynamic general equilibrium analogue of the dismal theorem applies. We show that, if the risk of climate tipping increases with temperature, the fat tail becomes endogenous and the dismal result is more likely to be activated at higher temperatures.

Title: The shape of U — On the structure of utility from electric vehicle charging
Authors: Philipp Theile
Abstract: With the growing adoption of electric vehicles, understanding user charging behavior is increasingly important for informing operational, investment, and policy decisions regarding their integration into the power system. While utility functions are commonly used to describe user preferences in charging behavior models, most existing studies rely on formulations with limited theoretical consistency and empirical validation, potentially leading to biased expectations.This paper empirically compares different utility function specifications and examines their implications for charging behavior modeling and charging station profitability.I introduce a novel discrete choice model framework to efficiently estimate utility function parameters from revealed preference data. Using a dataset of observed charging sessions at public charging stations in Germany, the model identifies accurate utility functions, uncovers charging preferences, and simulates station segment viability.The results suggest that charging utility is non-linear: marginal utility decreases with charged energy and marginal disutility increases with charging duration. An interaction between energy and duration leads to higher marginal valuation of energy for longer charging durations. Stations profit from inelastic demand driven by users who highly value energy content, are less price sensitive, and engage in high-value activities at the charging location, such as in urban areas or traffic hubs.

Title: Integrated production and truck–drone collaborative delivery scheduling problem to minimise the makespan
Authors: Lin Yuan, Zhaohong Jia, Yumei Huo
Affiliations: Anhui University; City University of New York
Abstract: This paper focuses on an integrated production and truck–drone collaborative delivery problem. The objective is to minimise the makespan. Jobs are first processed on a single machine in the factory and then distributed to their respective customers through a truck–drone pair in a back-and-forth manner. Specifically, the truck transports the processed jobs to the customer area, and at the parking point, the drone with limited flight endurance is launched to complete the final delivery to specific customer locations. Given that drone flight times vary across jobs, the general problem is shown to be strongly NP-hard. We identify two special cases that can be solved in polynomial time: (i) all jobs share the same drone flight time, and (ii) the number of distinct drone flight times is fixed. For both cases, we develop optimal algorithms. For the general case, we propose an approximation algorithm that integrates the First Fit Decreasing algorithm with Johnson's rule. Comprehensive numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Title: Vehicle routing for on-site services with time window flexibility and time-dependent speeds to minimise emission cost
Authors: Yizi Zhou, Jiyin Liu, Rupal Mandania
Affiliations: Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.; People’s Republic of China; Loughborough University
Abstract: We study the problem of scheduling engineers who drive to customer sites to perform service tasks. Vehicle speeds and associated CO2 emissions are time-dependent. Customers specify a service time window or choose to participate in a green delivery programme by offering multiple available time windows. This new vehicle routing problem with multiple time windows and time-dependent speeds is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to minimise emission costs. The model is then extended to handle scenarios in which customers can offer optional time windows on different days. To solve large instances, we develop a self-adaptive simulated annealing algorithm. For small instances solvable by optimisation software, experimental results show that the algorithm produces near-optimal solutions efficiently. Experiments on instances of different sizes show consistent improvement of the proposed algorithm over the standard simulated annealing. The algorithm is further applied in additional experiments simulating more practical operations. Results demonstrate that incorporating time window flexibility can reduce emission costs and increase the number of customers served under overbooking conditions. Tests under various settings indicate that greater participation in the green delivery programme, or more available time windows per customer, leads to further reductions in emission costs and improved service capacity.

Title: A multi-task dynamic deep survival network for corporate bond default prediction
Authors: Feng Shen, You Hu, Yuexing Tan, Kexin Yang
Affiliations: School of Finance, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics; Artificial Intelligence and Digital Finance Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Existing default prediction models predominantly focus on estimating the probability of default (PD) within fixed time horizons, often neglecting the time-to-default (TTD). While survival analysis captures TTD distributions, it implicitly assumes that all samples will eventually experience the event (i.e., default), which is often unrealistic in bond markets. To address this limitation, we propose the Multi-Task Dynamic Deep Survival Network (MT-DDSN), a joint learning framework that simultaneously predicts both PD and TTD. Operating as a multi-task framework, MT-DDSN unifies the default classification and survival analysis tasks through coordinated optimisation of prediction, likelihood, and ranking losses, thereby mitigating the error accumulation risks inherent in mixture cure models. Additionally, a feature-sharing layer acts as an information-constraining channel, facilitating continuous interaction between PD and TTD tasks to enhance representational capacity and model robustness. Furthermore, MT-DDSN integrates Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with a temporal attention mechanism. This architecture dynamically reweights LSTM hidden states to capture long-term temporal dependencies in bond and firm-level features, effectively mapping the complex transition of default risk from latent accumulation to observable exposure. Empirical evaluations using bond data from Chinese listed firms demonstrate that MT-DDSN outperforms baseline models in predicting both PD and TTD across various maturity segments.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Leveraging online reviews for customer regional preference demand analysis: evidence from Chinese new energy vehicle reviews
Authors: Peng Wu, Shuai Chen, Muhammet Deveci
Affiliations: School of Business, Anhui University; School of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Science and Technology; Department of Industrial Engineering, Turkish Naval Academy, National Defence University; University College London; Western Caspian University
Abstract: Regional preference demand analysis can help enterprises timely capture emerging demands and trends in different regions, thereby promoting product innovation and optimising marketing strategies. However, existing research neglects the impact of regional features on customer demand preferences. To address it, this paper proposes an analytical framework of customer regional demand preference by developing a lexicon-based sentiment analysis method of online reviews and two-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA). We first develop a lexicon-based sentiment analysis method by constructing a sentiment dictionary and an auxiliary dictionary to define sentiment values regarding these attributes of individual online review. Then, considering decision-making psychology of customer, the sentiment values are adjusted based on prospect theory, and customer satisfaction is subsequently defined using adjusted sentiment values. Furthermore, customer demand preference is analysed from feature demand preference and product demand preference using two-factor ANOVA, in which regional feature mainly contains city level and geographic region. Finally, we perform an experiment using customers’ historical data collected from Autohome to explore customer regional demand preferences.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Investment under uncertainty and the threat of nationalisation
Authors: Dimitrios Zormpas
Affiliations: University of Macedonia
Abstract: This paper considers the case of a multinational corporation which holds the option to invest in a foreign country. The company incurs the investment cost and gains access to a volatile profit flow once the project becomes operational. Apart from the uncertain market conditions, the investor must also account for the threat of nationalisation by the local government. By employing a dynamic model that incorporates both market uncertainty and political risk we determine the optimal timing for investment and nationalisation, as well as the appropriate scale of the investment. We show that a greater nationalisation threat leads to smaller but also earlier investment. Our findings provide a theoretical explanation for the empirical observation that investors do not necessarily avoid industries susceptible to nationalisation. We argue that the threat of nationalisation leads to premature and undersized investments, rather than deterring them entirely.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Exploring omni-channel bullwhip effect: The role of channel integration and consumer channel preference
Authors: Shiyu Liu, Yue Zhang, Jun Wang, Jinxing Hao, Ou Liu
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Beihang University; Petrochina(Beijing) Digital Intelligence Research Institute Co., LTD.; School of Reliability and System Engineering, Beihang University; Key Lab Complex Syst Anal Management & Decis, Minist Educ; Business School, Shenzhen Technology University
Abstract: The bullwhip effect is a prevalent phenomenon in supply chain management. With the emergence of omni-channel retailing, the structure of the supply chain has become more complex, leading to increased management challenges. In this paper, we aim to measure the bullwhip effect of an omni-channel supply chain with both offline and online channels and explore the impact of consumer channel preference and channel integration on the bullwhip effect. We set up a closed-form expression of the omni-channel bullwhip effect in which the retailer exhibits a price-sensitive demand model with a first-order autoregressive uniform pricing process, and the order-up-to level is calculated based on future demand forecast. Through mathematical and numerical analysis, we find that channel integration degree has a positive effect on reducing the omni-channel bullwhip effect, while the effect of consumer channel preference on the omni-channel bullwhip effect increases and then decreases. By comparing the omni-channel bullwhip effect with the single-channel one, we identify conditions under which effective consumer channel preference and channel integration strategies can reduce the omni-channel bullwhip effect. Finally, some suggestions for omni-channel retailers on market selection and channel integration strategies are presented to help them control the bullwhip effect at a lower level.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The conceptual HABITS prototype for integrating behavioural theories with system dynamics and agent-based models to capture complex health behaviours
Authors: Le Khanh Ngan Nguyen, Craig Donnachie, Susan Howick, Lynn Williams, Eunice Twumwaa Adwubi, Catriona Ewart, Min Hui Ang, Vahid Hajiebrahimi Farashah, Kristine Heimdal, Shafkat Ibrahimy, Itamar Megiddo
Affiliations: University of Strathclyde; Newcastle University; University of Glasgow; University of York
Abstract: Healthcare simulation models often rely on oversimplified assumptions about health behaviour, potentially undermining their predictive power and policy relevance. This paper systematically reviews how behavioural theories have been incorporated into healthcare simulation models and proposes HABITS (Health Behaviour Integrated Theory-based Simulation), a conceptual prototype combining advances in simulation modelling and behavioural science. Our research reveals that current approaches suffer from ad-hoc theory selection, overemphasis on behaviour change initiation over maintenance, and neglect of crucial areas, including health systems management, non-communicable-disease self-management, and provider behaviours. Most studies target motivation and opportunity drivers of health behaviour while overlooking capacity enhancement and broader social determinants. HABITS is designed to address these limitations by integrating the COM-B (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour) model with hybrid simulation approaches, providing structured guidance for incorporating behavioural determinants across system, social, and individual levels while capturing between-level feedback. This integration enables operationalisation of the Behaviour Change Wheel, allowing systematic development and evaluation of interventions and policies. This prototype aims to enhance design transparency, facilitate cross-study comparisons, and improve communication across disciplines and with stakeholders. Future research should explore theory-data integration and synergies between behavioural theories and emerging technologies such as Large Language Models to develop more robust, predictive models.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Monitoring and delivering: Evidence from dropout rates in Brazil
Authors: Bruno Kömel

Title: The youth dividend: Political impacts of demographic transitions
Authors: Rédha Chaba, Michael T. Dorsch, Victor Hiller, Paul Maarek
Abstract: This paper revisits the political economy of transitions to democracy. We extend a canonical rational choice model of democratization by introducing demographic structure, arguing that it shapes the material incentives for political mobilization. Younger cohorts benefit from democratic change over a longer horizon and face lower costs of participation, as they are less economically and socially integrated. As a result, increases in the youth share–such as during the demographic transition–can create a “window of opportunity” for democratization by strengthening the threat of political unrest faced by autocratic elites. We test this prediction using country-year panel data with detailed information on population age structure. Fixed-effects regressions reveal a robust positive relationship between the youth share and the likelihood of democratic improvement. This effect is strongest for the youngest cohorts, in particular individuals aged 15–19. To address concerns about endogeneity, we implement an instrumental variable strategy based on lagged fertility, including variation from neighboring countries. The IV estimates are consistent with the baseline results and are interpreted with appropriate caution. We also show that the effect of the youth share is amplified during economic downturns, highlighting a complementarity between demographic and macroeconomic forces.

Title: The Green Revolution and individualism: Evidence from Indonesia
Authors: Yeonha Jung, Uyseok Lee, Gedeon Lim
Abstract: This paper studies the effects of the Green Revolution, one of the largest development projects in the late 20th-Century, on individualism. We use a difference-in-differences approach to investigate how rapid technological and organizational changes in traditional agriculture reshaped cultural norms in Indonesia, where Green Revolution rollout was largely driven by centralized government interventions. Regions with greater exposure to Green Revolution policies experienced significant and persistent increases in individualism (as measured by a higher prevalence of infrequent names) decades after the end of the program. Results are not driven by pre-trends and hold across a battery of robustness checks. We further document suggestive, correlational evidence of a persistent fall in community funding for public goods, a key measure of collective action. Our findings suggest that technical change can lead to rapid and persistent changes in culture.

Title: Suing the leviathan: The effect of trans-regional jurisdiction reform on corporate investment
Authors: Jiayi Geng, Yinyi Jiao, Jinjun (Ricky) Ke, Meiting Lu, Yaowen Shan
Abstract: We study how the Trans-Regional Jurisdiction reform (TRJ) affects corporate investment. The reform moves administrative lawsuits to courts outside the defendant government's home jurisdiction, which limits local government influence over the courts. We use a stacked difference-in-differences design that draws on the staggered rollout of the reform across cities. We find that the reform raises corporate investment by about 28.7 percent of the sample mean. Complementary evidence shows that the reform improves court outcomes for firms, has stronger effects where pre-reform trust in local institutions is higher, and is associated with lower institutional transaction costs and financing constraints. The effect is larger for firms with more irreversible investment, lower state ownership, and better access to finance. The reform also leads firms to acquire more land and take on more risk, although part of the higher investment appears as overinvestment. These results show how a focused judicial reform can change firm behavior where legal institutions are weak.

Title: Data monetization strategy of two-sided platform concerning privacy concerns: Protection or compensation
Authors: Shuai Ling, Zhixin Deng, Jiyuan Guo

Title: The new energy vehicle’s research and development competition with technology uncertainty under dual credit policy
Authors: Zhiying Tao, Jianbin Li, Jihong Zhang, Zhaohua Wang

Title: The UK’s middle-income dietary trap: High emissions, low nutrition
Authors: Yunhuan Gao, Pablo Piñero, Eduardo Aguilera, Martin Bruckner, Alberto Sanz Cobeña, He He, Christian Reynolds
Abstract: Dietary transitions driven by income disparity increasingly impose a dual burden on health and the climate. This study integrates the Nutrient Rich Food (NRF 9.3 ) index and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate the nutrition‑carbon trade-off in UK household food purchases in 2013. Our analysis reveals a “middle-income dietary trap”. Across Deciles 4–8, households increase their overall food purchases as income rises, but this expansion is dominated by carbon-intensive, nutrient-poor foods such as meats, dairy, sugars, and vegetable oils. As a consequence, calorie intake peaks while improvements in diet quality lag behind, and carbon emissions reach their highest levels among all income groups. This misalignment reflects a stage in which rising food quantity precedes nutritional gains, generating a dual burden of high‑carbon, low-nutrition diets. In contrast, high-income groups (Deciles 9–10) achieve modest improvements in both nutrition and carbon efficiency, associated with higher consumption of nutrient-dense, low-GWP foods such as vegetables, fruits, and seafood. These findings highlight a non-linear income-emission relationship, consistent with the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis. Our decomposition analysis identifies two mechanisms shaping dietary carbon efficiency: a static opposition between expenditure and energy density, and a dynamic trade-off between nutrient density and the carbon intensity of nutrients. Policy interventions should adopt stage-specific strategies targeting middle-income households, where the dietary trap is driven by expenditure–structure imbalance, by steering substitution toward nutrient-dense, lower-carbon foods and accelerating structural dietary change.

Title: Climate change skepticism and farmers' responses to CO2e taxation
Authors: Kahsay Haile Zemo, Mette Termansen
Abstract: Agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet it has largely been exempt from stricter environmental regulations, partly due to strong resistance from the sector. Across Europe, farmers' widespread opposition has often resulted in the weakening or rollback of ambitious environmental policies. In Denmark, the recent introduction of a CO2e (CO2-equivalent) tax on agricultural emissions, one of the first global attempts to directly target non-fossil fuel-based GHGs, has similarly prompted immediate organized farmer protests. This study examines whether and to what extent climate change skepticism (CCS) is associated with farmers' belief misalignment about the economic impact of the CO2e tax on agriculture, resistance to the tax, and adoption of climate mitigation measures, drawing on a survey of 981 Danish farmers. We find that climate skeptic farmers substantially overestimate the tax's negative impacts while discounting expert assessments. Climate neutral and skeptic farmers show greater opposition to the CO2e tax, with CCS strongly predicting resistance even after accounting for tax design, information, and farm characteristics. Higher CCS is also associated with lower adoption of climate mitigation measures, with participation in subsidized climate initiatives about 25% lower among skeptics compared with non-skeptics. These patterns are more pronounced among livestock producers than crop producers. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of climate-related beliefs in explaining variation in beliefs about policy impacts, policy acceptance, and behavioral responses.

Title: Preferences for wealth accumulation and wealth inequality: Experimental evidence
Authors: Nobuyuki Hanaki, Yuta Shimodaira

Title: A practical approach to multi-day dynamic pricing in attended home delivery
Authors: Hsin Kai Huang, Ryota Okazaki, Yuki Oyama
Abstract: This paper proposes a sampling-based dynamic pricing approach for attended home delivery (AHD), utilizing approximation methods to improve both calculation efficiency and profitability. First, the pricing mechanism is formulated as a choice-based optimization to reflect individual customer preferences. To account for the sequential arrival of multiple customers, the problem is extended to a Markov decision process (MDP) framework. For practical use, a logistics platform must determine prices within 100 milliseconds to ensure a seamless experience for each customer. However, the computational complexity of vehicle routing combined with future uncertainty regarding multi-day customer choices leads to the curse of dimensionality, making real-time application computationally infeasible. To address these challenges, we introduce area-based (Continuous Approximation and Regression-based) and route-based (Cheapest Insertion) approximation methods. Crucially, a sampling-based approximation is developed to mitigate future uncertainty across multi-day delivery options, thereby overcoming the computational barriers of the MDP framework. The performance of each method is evaluated via simulation, incorporating a nested logit model estimated from large-scale stated choice data to reflect realistic delivery timing preferences. The results show that dynamic pricing outperforms fixed pricing, with all methods meeting the required speed limitations (100 milliseconds). After integrating the sampling-based model, profits increase across all approximation methods. Additionally, we evaluate the model under different cost-scaling factors, slot capacities, and customer preferences. The results show that sampling-based policies generally improve profit, with route-based approximation maintaining the highest average profit across the tested settings. This efficient approach provides a scalable and robust solution for dynamic time slot pricing in real-world logistics platforms.

Title: Modeling a resilient port industry and logistics system under global geopolitical and economic uncertainties
Authors: Zhongbin Zhao, Zhenhang Zhou, Jihong Chen, Mengru Shen, Hao Wang, Kee-hung Lai, Chuan Pang, Dairong Wang

Title: Public transit funding and transit use: a panel study of U.S. urbanized areas 2010–2019
Authors: Pengyu Zhu, Zining Wang, Xuan Zhang, Kailai Wang

Title: Transit-induced household migration: A survival analysis of heterogeneous income effects near urban rail corridors
Authors: Adam Schmidt, Eleni Bardaka
Abstract: Urban rail investments can reshape neighborhood demographics, yet the timing and magnitude of any displacement pressures remain poorly documented. This study develops a methodological framework that links annual, household-level consumer microdata with quasi-experimental design to (i) trace in- and out-migration near new light-rail stations, (ii) explore the sociodemographic profile of moving households, and (iii) estimate how proximity, project milestones, and household income interact to change the risk of households migrating out of their neighborhoods. Our econometric analysis includes survival models with two alternative timescales, two control areas, and estimation of heterogeneous impacts by household income level. We illustrate the method with a case study of Charlotte’s LYNX Original and Extension of the Blue Line, drawing on a 16-year panel of 437,606 geocoded households. For the Original line, our results show a 4-5% increase in the probability of low- and medium-income households exiting from their neighborhood 5–9 years after the light rail began operating but no long-term effect. On the newer Extension, low- and middle-income households were 6-10% less likely to move out in the first four years after the light rail began operating. However, the share of low-income residents living near stations still declined, mainly due to medium-income household in-migration. Our findings highlight important lessons for policymakers. First, displacement pressure can surface years after opening; second, net demographic shifts often arise from selective in-migration rather than disproportionate exits; and third, equity measures must combine long-term anti-displacement policies with tools that preserve affordability and social mix in new development near transit.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How effective are narrative messages in changing attitudes and preferences for electric vehicles? A before-and after stated choice experiment
Authors: Cristian Domarchi, Elisabetta Cherchi, Quoc C. Vuong
Abstract: Attitudinal change is an important factor in increasing electric vehicle (EV) acceptance and accelerating market adoption. In this paper we aim to understand the processes underlying changes in attitudes and preferences towards EVs by examining individual responses to narrative-based persuasion messages, which have been shown in psychological research as an effective technique to change attitudes. To represent the diversity of information individuals may encounter, we investigate the role of appeal (rational vs. emotional) and type (positive vs. negative) in messages. We analyse data from a “before-and-after” stated choice (SC) experimental survey, administered to a sample of vehicle owners in England. Participants first completed an SC experiment and an attitudinal questionnaire. In a follow-up survey, respondents allocated to experimental groups were exposed to a narrative-based message about EVs before repeating the SC experiment and attitudinal questionnaire, while a control group received no messages. Our findings confirm that participants respond more strongly to positive information about EVs than to negative messages. We also find that the adverse impact of unfavourable messaging about EVs can be partially mitigated by providing positive information. Overall, our results show that narrative messages can be effective in changing attitudes and preferences toward EVs, contrasting with the outcomes typically observed with advocacy-based messages. These results can therefore help shape policy measures to support the transition toward sustainable mobility.

Title: High-speed rail, expressways, and revitalization after the Great East Japan Earthquake

Title: Distributional welfare impacts and compensatory transit strategies under NYC congestion pricing

Title: A batch approximate evaluation method for neighborhood solutions in job shop scheduling
Authors: Zhiyong Ba, Jinduo Liu, Yiping Yuan

Title: Consumable data via quantum communication
Authors: Dar Gilboa, Siddhartha Jain, Jarrod R. McClean
Abstract: Classical data can be copied and re-used for computation, with adverse consequences economically and in terms of data privacy. Motivated by this, we formulate problems in one-way communication complexity where Alice holds some data x and Bob holds m inputs y 1 , … , y m . They want to compute m instances of a bipartite relation R ( · , · ) on every pair ( x , y 1 ) , … , ( x , y m ) . We call this the asymmetric direct sum question for one-way communication. We give examples where the quantum communication complexity of such problems scales polynomially with m , while the classical communication complexity depends at most logarithmically on m . Thus, for such problems, data behaves like a consumable resource that is effectively destroyed upon use when the owner stores and transmits it as quantum states, but not when transmitted classically. We show an application to a strategic data-selling game, and discuss other potential economic implications.
